articles.title: CRASH Network’s Insurer Report Card Survey Now Open
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: CRASH Network announced that its annual “Insurer Report Card” survey is now open. By taking the survey, collision repairers can help consumers choose a better auto insurer by sharing their firsthand knowledge of how different carriers handle claims.

More than 1,000 collision repair professionals participate each year, grading insurers doing business in their state from “A+” to “F” based on how well each company’s claims practices help ensure quality repairs and customer service.

“Most consumers probably aren’t aware that they likely have dozens and dozens of companies from which they could buy their auto insurance policy,” said John Yoswick, editor of CRASH Network. “Through the Insurer Report Card, collision repairers can share what they see in their shops every day to help consumers realize there are differences among carriers beyond just price and brand recognition, and to help introduce consumers to insurers they may not have previously been familiar with.”

The results reach consumers throughout the year. In addition to being available for free download, the grades are incorporated into auto insurance rankings from more than a dozen sources such as the Wall Street Journal, Money and USA Today. Insurers that consistently receive top grades also tout those results in their own consumer marketing.

“The Insurer Report Card allows repairers to grade 20 or 30 insurers doing business in their state,” Yoswick said. “Because of that, we’re able to show consumers grades received by about 80 or more different carriers.”

The Insurer Report Card can be completed in less than three minutes (though shops are encouraged to spend time to explain why they gave each insurer the grade they did), and all individual shop grades and identification information remains confidential.
Shops that complete the Insurer Report Card and provide an e-mail address will be sent the results at no charge to share with their customers.
To request a link to the survey, shops can click here.

articles.title: All Clear Diagnostics & Calibration Expands into Colorado

Its continued market expansion reflects the company’s commitment to supporting customers as vehicle technology and repair requirements evolve.

articles.title: Intrepid and Kinetic program will give premium discounts for ADAS procedures performed
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: A new program launched by Intrepid Direct and Kinetic ID could reduce business insurance costs for collision repair shops that recognize and complete ADAS procedures.

Nikhil Naikal, CEO and co-founder of Kinetic, told Repairer Driven News that the software is used by shops and insurance carriers to identify ADAS requirements when vehicles have been in a collision or if they had a mechanical repair done.

“Sensors on the vehicles can be disrupted or dislodged during the process of a repair and the requirements of calibrations are not very easy to know or understand,” Naikal said. “It is a hidden digital damage. Kinetic ID is a software that helps identify when reprogramming and calibrations are required.”
Intrepid Direct, which provides business insurance to collision repair facilities, have identified that the completion of proper ADAS procedures serves as a liability risk control, Naikal said.

“Collision repair keeps getting more complex, and shops are being asked to take responsibility for increasingly sophisticated vehicle systems,” Bill Strout, president of Intrepid Direct, says in a press release. “This program gives our customers an easy way to build systematic ADAS review into their estimating and repair workflows through Kinetic ID Premium. Just as important, it creates a way to recognize shops that consistently identify and complete the right ADAS procedures, because those practices help reduce repair risk.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Through the use of Kinetic ID software, collision shops can qualify for additional liability and umbrella premium discounts, Naikal said. He adds that Intrepid Direct sees more use of the software and performance of ADAS calibrations as risk reducing behavior by the collision repair business.

“Their completed operations exposure goes down, and umbrella claims can go down,” Naikal adds. “Intrepid is recognizing that positive behavior and willing to reward that behavior with additional discounts.”
Identifying calibrations is important for vehicle repair, Naikal added.

“These sensors on the cars are no longer just convenience features,” he says. “They’re safety features. A vehicle that’s driving down the freeway at 60 miles per hour with a miscalibrated lane-keeping or lane-assist sensor behind the windshield or a blind spot monitoring system that doesn’t alert oncoming traffic in an adjacent lane can cause an accident and can be life-threatening for both the driver and passengers as well as the other vehicle.”
Failing to calibrate sensors can leave a vehicle not returned to its original state of safety, Naikal adds.
Naikal notes that Kinetic is a starting point that repair shops should use.

“The repairer is the one who has to make these decisions, and it could be nuanced,” Naikal said. “It could be circumstances and instances that they would choose to go one way or the other. Our idea with the software is to give them a starting point on the research and on where to go look.”

The partnership is a sign that the broader industry is recognizing good repair behavior, he adds. Shops that bring vehicles back to the factory state of safety will be rewarded for that behavior, he says.
“This is a good thing that the broader industry is starting to recognize shops that go the extra mile and make sure that the cars are repaired correctly,” Naikal says.

During a Collision Industry Conference meeting earlier this year, Rebekah Cooper, The Cooper Firm partner, explained how improper repairs, including those that involve ADAS systems, can be deadly or cause serious injuries.

Improper repair cases are changing as more emerging technology, such as ADAS features, become prominent on vehicles, she said. She said the legal system currently sees dozens of ADAS cases annually and that number is expected to increase.
She told the story of a case where a repair involving a bumper necessitated a calibration that wasn’t completed by the repair shop.

The firm discovered this by looking at what technology was on the vehicle and the repair procedures to see how it’s supposed to be repaired. They tracked the vehicle back to the last place it was repaired. It was discovered the business didn’t do the needed repair, she said.

The failed repair caused the collision warning not to work, she said. The consumer was quadriplegic following the crash. She lived in a mobile home for three years waiting for accountability, Cooper added.

“There are times we ask a shop for those, and the OEM has it, but the shop does not,” Cooper said. “Have you seen this before? When is the first time? Are you seeing it for the first time right now? If the answer is yes, that’s a problem.”

Intrepid and Kinetic’s new program will also give Intrepid Direct collision repair customers a limited-time free trial of Kinetic ID Premium and provide Kinetic network shops with access to Intrepid Direct insurance.
The program will kick off with Kinetic and Intrepid Direct co-hosting an event at Wynn Las Vegas Tuesday, Nov. 3 at 6 p.m. during the SEMA Show.
The Society of Collision Repair Specialists’ (SCRS) 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit will dive into a conversation about ADAS and calibrations during the SEMA Show next week.

The afternoon begins with “The National Safety Objective: Safer Vehicles, Safer Roads,” featuring National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) Deputy Administrator Lee White, who will examine federal vehicle and roadway safety priorities.

The session, held Thursday, Nov. 5 from 12:30-1:30 p.m., will include a conversation about emerging transportation technologies, data-driven research, and the federal government’s work with the industry to reduce fatalities and serious injuries, an SCRS release states.

During the “Engineering the Safety Benefit: From Requirements to Real-World Performance” session, active safety engineers from General Motors and Rivian will provide a look behind the engineering decisions that influence vehicle safety before, during, and after a collision.

The session, held Thursday, Nov. 5, from 2–3 p.m., will explore ADAS feature development, real-world effectiveness, crash avoidance and mitigation, implications of inoperable systems, verification of safety performance, and the potential for system degradation.

A session that follows, “Preserving the Driver Assistance System: Sensors, Calibration and Repairability,” will include service engineering experts from General Motors, Ford Motor Co., and Rivian. The conversation will answer for repairers what it takes to preserve and restore ADAS capabilities engineered into the vehicle after collisions.
The session, held Thursday, Nov. 5, from 3:30–4:30 p.m., will also take attendees behind the development of collision repair information.
The 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit is part of SCRS’ Repairer Driven Education (RDE) program at the SEMA Show, which includes several classes, the IDEAS Collide Showcase, and more.

An SCRS RDE Full Series Pass provides access to Tuesday and Wednesday RDE sessions, IDEAS Collide, the OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit, and the SCRS Afterparty. To register for the full series pass, click here.

articles.title: JD Power says total losses weigh on insurance customer satisfaction
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: Auto insurance customer satisfaction with claims handling practices depends on repairability, according to a new study from JD Power.
According to the 2026 U.S. Auto Claims Satisfaction Study, total loss determinations decrease overall customer satisfaction by 12 points.

The study shows that overall customer satisfaction with the auto insurance claims process improves 4 points (on a 1,000-point scale) when damages are repairable. This is the third consecutive year of declining satisfaction for total loss claims, declining 46 points since 2023.

Overall, 26% of auto insurance claims were classified as total losses in 2026, up from just 16% four years ago. JD Power notes that vehicle repairs have become more costly, more customers are keeping their vehicles on the road longer, and higher deductibles are removing smaller repairs from the claim process.

The overall auto claims customer satisfaction score is the same as last year at 700. Amica ranks highest in overall customer satisfaction at 775, followed by Nationwide (743) and Automobile Club of Southern CA (AAA) (740).

“A complex mix of trends are conspiring to make this an incredibly challenging market environment for managing auto insurance claims customer satisfaction,” said Mark Garrett, JD Power’s director of global insurance intelligence, in the press release.

“On the positive side, rates are coming down and repair cycle times have improved dramatically, so customers who can have their vehicles fixed are showing high levels of satisfaction with the claims experience. However, persistent affordability challenges have many customers keeping vehicles longer or making changes to their policy, such as dropping rental coverage or taking on higher insurance deductibles. Additionally, many customers are upside down on their auto loans, which means the payoff in a total loss scenario can be less than they owe on their vehicles. All of these can make for a poor customer experience in the event of a total loss.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Total loss customer satisfaction scores are lowest (490) when insurer payouts don’t cover what the customer still owes on their vehicle loan, according to the study. Among total loss customers with vehicle loans, 25% received payouts that were less than what they owed.
JD Power notes that repair cycle times are improving, down to 15.3 days through Q1 and 10 days less than in Q1 2024.
In August, Enterprise Mobility reported that the overall length of rental (LOR) for collision-related rentals in Q2 2026 was 15.1 days, the same as Q2 2025.

Overall customer satisfaction scores are highest (804) when customers completely agree that their insurer provided a seamless experience across channels. Satisfaction scores are lowest (390) when customers disagree with that statement. Disagreement often comes from not understanding explanations, using multiple channels to ask questions, or digital tools not working as expected, according to JD Power.
“Currently, insurers are delivering a seamless cross-channel experience just 54% of the time, one of the lowest-performing key performance indicators in the study,” JD Power says.

The study examines trust, fairness of settlement, people, time to settle a claim, communication, ease of resolving a claim, ease of starting a claim, and digital channels in auto claims experiences of customers from the largest insurance providers across the U.S.

The 2026 study is based on survey responses from 8,261 auto insurance customers who settled a claim within the past nine months before responding to the survey. The survey was fielded from September 2025 through August 2026.

articles.title: Cox Automotive VinSolutions, Honda investigate suspicious cyber activity
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: Cox Automotive confirmed Friday that it recently “detected suspicious activity” in VinSolutions, its CRM and sales software, while Honda said it is investigating a separate recent cybersecurity incident. Neither company provided dates of the incidents.
CBT News reported Oct. 27 that hackers, calling themselves Scarlett Group, posted “claims” involving VinSolutions online Oct. 23.

“However, Cox hasn’t confirmed those claims, and they remain unverified,” the article states. “Ransomware.live recorded Scarlett Group’s listing of VinSolutions on its leak site Friday [Oct. 23], describing the group as newly active and saying its claims should be treated with caution until independently verified. Dark web monitoring service Darkwiser reported that the group claims to have customer records, including Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers, and credit applications. Notably, Darkwiser labeled the claims unverified, and Cox hasn’t confirmed any data types or published a record count.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Honda confirmed to RDN that it recently experienced a cybersecurity incident involving its Interactive Network (iN).

“As a precaution, Honda temporarily took the iN offline to allow for a proper investigation and ensure the protection of our system,” Honda spokesperson Chris Naughton told RDN on Friday. “At this time, we have not identified evidence that customer information was accessed, and our investigation remains ongoing. Honda was able to safely restore iN services on Wednesday (10/28/26).”

A collision repair shop received an email on Oct. 29 from a Honda dealership saying that a cybersecurity attack compromised Honda iN, preventing more than 1,100 dealerships nationwide from checking inventory availability and placing new parts orders.
Separately, an anonymous tip provided to RDN indicated some collision centers have been compromised through email links, allowing threat actors to access CCC’s estimating and management systems.

They said once the link is clicked, threat actors access and change passwords in the systems, then use them to contact insurance companies posing as collision centers, saying the customer removed the vehicle, or that the insurance company should just pay the customer, and provide updated account information.
They’ve also reportedly called an insurance company, posing as the customer, and said they aren’t getting the vehicle repaired and want to cash out.
CCC didn’t confirm or deny the tip. However, CCC shared information about the security advisories it provides to shops to help protect themselves.

“This is an important topic,” said Michelle Hellyar, CCC spokesperson. “Email phishing, social engineering, and impersonation scams are an increasing threat across industries. Like many technology providers, CCC periodically shares security advisories and best practices to help customers recognize and avoid these attacks. These advisories are preventive in nature and not prompted by a compromise of CCC’s systems.

“In our advisories, we encourage businesses to use multi-factor authentication, never share passwords, exercise caution with unexpected requests involving sensitive information or payment changes, and independently verify those requests through established, trusted contacts before taking action.”
Last year, IT services company StoredTech simulated the ramifications of a fictional cybersecurity attack on an auto repair shop for attendees of a Collision Industry Conference (CIC) meeting.

In the scenario, the owner replied to an email that he thought was from his trusted supplier, “Tool Titans.” The email asked for information to complete a tool order and included multi-factor authentication.
Allan Polak, StoredTech senior of technology, said the hackers threatened to permanently delete all of Bob’s data and leak it to the dark web if half a Bitcoin wasn’t paid within 72 hours.
Polak guided the audience through Bob’s decision to pay the ransom after three days of no business operations.

“Threat actors used the stolen passwords to gain access to multiple computers in Bob’s office, and they gained access to other resources, like phones, cloud, files, et cetera,” Polak said. “And once they gained access to those computers, they also found an Excel spreadsheet. That Excel spreadsheet was a treasure trove. It had all kinds of passwords for them, including some personal accounts, and they use that to just gain a larger foothold and go deeper and deeper.”

articles.title: College Students Build Skills — and a Bronco – At SEMA
articles.author: Matthew Simpson

paras.en: At this year’s SEMA Show, we are turning customization into a live, hands-on experience. Attendees will be able to use the Ford Custom Garage 3D configurator onsite to design their dream Ford Bronco with Ford Accessories and Ford Racing Parts in our inaugural Ford Custom Garage Ultimate Build Competition. Then, six Washtenaw Community College (WCC) students will bring the winning design to life on the show floor, building the Bronco live in our booth before it is revealed on the final day of the show.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That show-floor build is the headline moment — and it is also the reason this program matters. Together with WCC, we created a semester-long experience that connects students to real vehicles, current tools, industry leaders, and the business of vehicle customization, giving them a role on one of the biggest stages in the automotive aftermarket.

At Ford, building the future of the automotive industry means investing in more than vehicles. It means investing in the people who will build, customize, service, and improve them. Our Ultimate Build at SEMA makes that investment visible, turning a classroom partnership into a public demonstration of student skill, creativity, and career potential.
A Semester of Learning, Access and Hands-On Work

Across eight weekly sessions from September through October, my Ford colleagues and our industry partners showed students how ideas move from concept to customer — and introduced the careers that make that work possible.

Our Ford Speaker Series covered the aftermarket and dealer business, product development, design, hands-on customization, original equipment manufacturer (OEM) personalization, the business behind Ford Customization and marketing for SEMA. Students heard directly from professionals across design, engineering, accessories, operations, and marketing.

We also loaned two Bronco SUVs and gave tools to the class, which made these lessons tangible. With guidance from instructors and working professionals, students inspected, diagnosed, disassembled, installed, and problem-solved on real vehicles — the kind of experience that connects classroom learning to the work happening every day across the industry.
The Ford Custom Garage Ultimate Build at SEMA

At SEMA, our Ford Custom Garage Ultimate Build invites attendees to take part in the process. Using an onsite 3D configurator, they can build their dream Ford Bronco. A panel will select 10 finalists, the public will vote for the winning design, and WCC students will build it live in our booth before revealing the completed Bronco to the public on the show’s final day.

The live build gives students a national stage, but it also gives them a demanding real-world assignment. Working on a compressed timeline, the students will draw on a semester of technical training and conversations about product development, design, personalization, business, and marketing.

SEMA is the capstone, not the whole story. The real value is in the preparation that gets them there — the technical practice, the exposure to working professionals and the confidence that comes from contributing to a vehicle thousands of people will see at SEMA.
“At Ford, building the future means investing in the people behind our vehicles, not just the vehicles themselves.”
Matt Simpson, Executive Director of Ford Customization

Our country faces a significant skilled-trades gap. According to a new report, “The Alliance for America’s Skilled-Trades: A National Report,” supported by BlackRock, Carhartt, Ford, and Google, more workers in the United States are aging out of skilled-trades jobs than are entering. Data shows that 24% of the trades workforce nationally is 55 or over and nearing an exit, while just 11% of workers are under 25.

Many young people value hands-on careers but do not always know what opportunities exist or how to enter these fields. This program helps close that distance by combining instruction, equipment, industry exposure, and a national platform where students can demonstrate their skills.
At Ford, we cannot close that gap alone, but we can work with strong educational partners to put vehicles and resources in students’ hands and connect training to real customer and business needs.

The six students were selected through a competitive application process, and they bring interests ranging from collision repair and refinishing to electrical systems, performance upgrades, custom fabrication, and mechanical engineering. They represent a broader WCC learning community that participated in the semester’s classes, vehicle work, and speaker sessions.

The winning Bronco will show more than how a Bronco can be customized. It will show what students can accomplish when they have access to real vehicles, current tools, relevant instruction, and working professionals who can help connect their skills to future careers.

At Ford Customization, and across the entire Ford Customer Service Division, we believe the customer relationship does not end when someone buys a Ford; it is just the start of the journey to make it their Ford. The relationship continues through the parts, accessories, service, and expertise that help owners make their vehicles work better for their lives.

Ford Custom Garage is one expression of that work, making personalization easier through Ford-engineered, tested and warranty-backed packages — but skilled people bring those packages to life. Our WCC partnership connects both sides: donated Broncos and tools support instruction, guest lecturers explain the work behind customization, and SEMA gives students a chance to apply their skills in public.

When the completed Bronco is revealed, the most important result will not only be the vehicle itself. It will be the learning behind it: new skills, professional relationships and a clearer view of the careers open to these students.

They are why we are investing in this program. They represent the talent and craftsmanship our industry needs and what is possible when education and industry work together to create sustained access to the skills, people, and opportunities that turn potential into a career.

articles.title: How Do We Recruit the Next Generation of Technicians?
articles.author: Christian Hinton

paras.en: The automotive industry faces a growing workforce challenge, making automotive technician recruitment increasingly important for repair shops. A wave of experienced technicians is nearing retirement, while the number of incoming workers is not large enough to replace them.
The industry needs tens of thousands of jobs filled each year. At the same time, training programs are not producing enough graduates, and Americans are keeping their vehicles longer.
Shops looking to close the labor gap need to reach the next generation of workers earlier and more effectively.
Automotive Technician Recruitment Can Reach New Candidates
Recruiting the next generation of technicians starts with reaching candidates where they are. That can include groups shops may not traditionally consider, such as recent college graduates.

Many young people are leaving college and entering a crowded job market. Some graduates may be open to different career paths, particularly those offering competitive pay, stability and an in-demand skill.
Employee-sponsored training and formal apprenticeship programs can help provide that path.
Job Postings Should Explain the Purpose of the Work

Younger workers also want to understand the purpose behind their work. They want to know who they are helping and why their role matters. For that reason, job postings should communicate more than the availability of an automotive technician position.

Cars are part of everyday life, and technicians help keep people moving. Shops are hiring employees who play a role in keeping vehicles on the road. Communicating that purpose can help candidates understand the broader value of the job.
Workplace Culture Can Support Technician Retention

Many young workers are accustomed to having options and experiencing rapid change. If a workplace does not meet their expectations, they may choose to leave rather than remain in the position. That makes workplace culture an important part of technician recruitment and retention.

Shops can build stronger relationships by taking an interest in employees’ lives and creating opportunities for teams to connect. Team events can also help employees become more comfortable with one another and feel more connected to the shop.

articles.title: Don’t Forget Lubrication During an Oil Change
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: Back in my day at the service station, when a customer came in for an oil change, they pulled it into a grease pit and we would grease up everything on the vehicle—ball joints, universal joints, and then we would do the oil changes. Today, it’s different. Vehicles are a lot more low maintenance.

However, the aftermarket has not abandoned the message that lubrication is required for certain repair components to make that repair just that much better. In other words, we have ball joints that have grease nipples that need to be lubricated every so often, like during an oil change. It’s also written in the vehicle service information that doors and lift hatches need to be lubricated every so often.
Your shop probably has an oil change and you probably call it an LOF. So let’s put that L back in LOF: lubrication, oil, filter.

articles.title: Are sharks really older than trees?
articles.author: Alice Sun

paras.en: You may have heard that sharks are older than trees. And yes, sharks are truly ancient, with an evolutionary lineage dating back hundreds of millions of years.
But are they really older than trees? Experts told Live Science that the answer depends on what we classify as a shark.

"It's all in the fine print," John Maisey, the curator-in-charge emeritus of fossil fish at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, told Live Science. "The takeaway is that the shark lineage within the fishes generally does go back further than trees. But it really depends on how you define what we mean by shark."

The modern sharks we see today first emerged around 195 million years ago, during the Jurassic period. Fossils of ancient sharks from this time can be traced to living lineages, namely Hexanchiformes, an order of sharks identified by their six or seven gills and single dorsal fin.

This means that modern sharks, at least, are not older than trees. Experts generally agree that trees first evolved in the Middle Devonian epoch, around 380 million to 390 million years ago. "I think it's not very controversial, when we had the first trees," Cindy Looy, a paleobotanist at the University of California, Berkeley, told Live Science.

For instance, the first true tree in the evolutionary record is considered to be Archaeopteris, an extinct genus discovered in a 385 million-year-old fossil forest near Cairo, New York. Looking at these fossils, Archaeopteris has many characteristics of trees we have today, including a tall, woody trunk; leaves; and a deep root system. Other early trees — such as Eospermatopteris found in ancient forests near Gilboa, New York, and Calamophyton in southwest England — also appeared in the fossil record 390 million and 393 million years ago, respectively.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But when we look at the extinct relatives of modern sharks, "that's where it gets a bit wobbly," Maisey said. There are fossils from the sister groups of modern sharks that can be traced back through the Permian period and into the Devonian period (around 359 million to 420 million years ago). The most abundant group are hybodonts, an extinct group of spiny fish that have a unique calcification pattern in their cartilage that is similar to that of modern sharks.
Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

"It’s called tessellated calcified cartilage, and that's a very important hallmark of most of the shark-like fishes and their ancestors," said Maisey, who has studied a spiny fish fossil called Doliodus problematicus from the early Devonian. If this definition is used, these sharks first appeared around 400 million years ago, before trees emerged.
Sharks' rough skin can be traced even further back, with the dermal denticles — the tooth-like scales that roughen a shark's skin — first appearing in the fossil record around 450 million years ago.

These transition fossils, where fish were evolving into sharks and gaining shark-like traits, introduce a gray area in the definition of sharks. "When you get back into the ancient past, when you're not dealing with things that we have living examples to compare with anymore, then it becomes a bit more tricky [to figure out what they are]," Maisey said.

Fossils also present a very limited picture. Many contain only fragments of an animal, like a fallen tooth, so scientists are still piecing together the clues of exactly how and when sharks arose. That means every fish fossil discovery often leads to more questions about what other transition fossils could be out there, Maisey said.

There is also much to be discovered about trees, Looy added. Terrestrial fossils, especially ones that clearly show parts of a tree, are quite rare. Finding a fossil forest requires a lot of luck, she said, although there is little indication that trees were present before the Middle Devonian.
"That's why I think the fossil record is so intriguing," Maisey said. "Because it may not give us all the answers, but it certainly raises questions."

Alice Sun is a science journalist based in Brooklyn. She covers a wide range of topics, including ecology, neuroscience, social science and technology. Her work has appeared in Audubon, Sierra, Inverse and more. For her bachelor's degree, she studied environmental biology at McGill University in Canada. She also has a master's degree in science, health and environmental reporting from NYU.

articles.title: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie
articles.author: Olivia Maule

paras.en: Most deception in nature happens without much awareness from the creature involved. From a moth that has evolved to look like a hornet to orchid mantises that mimic flowers to lure in pollinators, deception is part of these animals' nature. But in his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), biologist James O'Hanlon turns to tactical deception aimed at manipulating what another animal believes — and whether we can consider this as lying.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Live Science spoke with O'Hanlon about his book, and why so many scientists are reluctant to say "yes, animals can lie."
Read an excerpt: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

Olivia Maule: The chapter opens with a moment from a talk you gave, where a woman at a senior citizens' club asked you a question about orchid mantises that left you stumped: "How does the mantis know to look like a flower?" Why did that moment stick with you enough to open the chapter with it?

James O'Hanlon: Because it was such a simple, straightforward question that I couldn't give a simple, straightforward answer to. At the time, I was thinking about what's going on in the brains of the animals I was looking at — does a camouflaged animal actually know it's camouflaged? Does an insect that looks like a leaf know what a leaf even is?

And it got me thinking: they don't need to. This stuff just sort of works because it works. That's a completely different type of deception to the other things dealt with in this chapter, which is: Do animals actually know that they can lie? Can they intentionally deceive, like we can?
OM: So would you say you have an answer to that question now? And if so, what would it be?

JO: If I had to answer, it would be yes. It looks like it. But scientists are paid to be pedantic, so it's always going to be a "yes, but" or a "possibly." There's a ton of behaviors that look like animals can lie, and they're really good at it, but with any type of science, we're never going to know for certain what's going on in their brains. It's a best-guess situation.
OM: How would you help readers hold those two ideas at once — that this is genuine deception in an evolutionary sense, but not necessarily lying in the way we mean it as humans?

JO: When we talk about lying in humans, there's a value judgment attached. We're judging each other on whether we're good or bad people, doing right or wrong things. We kind of have to relax that judgment a bit when we're talking about other animals.

I guess it becomes an ethical question — we look at deception as being right or wrong, morally good or bad, and that's a very human-centric way of thinking. Ethics and morals are things we've developed to help us get along in our own societies. Who knows what's going on in animal societies?

There's an example in the book of golden snub-nosed monkeys that use deceptive alarm calls to scare off other members of their group and steal their food. After a while, those monkeys start to get ignored, and the group stops responding to their calls. So maybe there is some sort of animal-society rules and regulations keeping lying in check. Maybe. We'll see.

OM: I do want to ask about the chimpanzee study, in which chimpanzees intentionally misled competitive handlers to boxes without food, and compare it to the 2017 dog study, where dogs learned to mislead handlers much faster than the chimps did. What did that result do to the assumption that big brains equal better lying?

JO: There's always been this idea that lying is a really cognitively complex task — you need the brains not just to realize what's going on in the real world but to imagine a false possibility, and then to describe that false possibility as if it were real. We talked that up as something you need big brains to do, and there was also a bit of patting ourselves on the back for being such smart animals — maybe we lie a lot because we're such smart animals. But the more we learn about animals and what they're capable of, the more we realize they can do so much more than we thought was possible with the brains they've got.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: OM: Does that suggest lying is less about raw intelligence and more a byproduct of needing to survive in a group?

JO: As far as all the examples of tactical deception in the book that look like they're intentional, they all, or mostly all, come from social animals. We don't seem to see it in solitary animals. That's a big sign that maybe it's something that's evolved because individuals can exploit it in a social setting. But it's still such early days, so it's hard to say for definite how different levels of sociality, and how bonded individuals are within groups, correlate with more deception.
OM: Could you elaborate on the distinction between deception and something like the camouflage you introduce in the book with the tiger's stripes?

JO: Compared to the intentional deception we've been talking about, things like camouflage still work regardless of whether the animal doing it is aware of it or not. The idea behind lying and tactical deception is that it only works because it's intentional — there's some sort of choice to do it.

Whether the animals are aware of that choice is another question. Think about the way we do it as humans — are we always aware of it? Whenever your friend asks whether you like their new haircut and you just go, "Yeah, it's great," you don't really think about the fact that you're probably lying. It's just part of our social norms. So it becomes a very blurry gray area very quickly.
OM: It sort of boils down to the choice of it all — whether they can choose to do it or not, which raises the question of whether it's conscious or unconscious.

JO: It's tricky, because as soon as you start talking about it being a conscious decision these animals make, you start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches, giggling at how evil they are for pretending to hide nuts. And you start to think, maybe this isn't the right exact way to think about lying and deception.

OM: The drongo — a bird renowned for its ability to deceive meerkats — doesn't just have one trick, it cycles through different alarm calls and borrows calls from other bird species. Does that put it in a different category of liar than squirrels or monkeys, or is it the same trick with a different toolbox?

JO: It could just be the same trick with a different toolbox. It's essentially doing the same thing as the golden snub-nosed monkeys we were talking about before. But birds are incredible singers and have very flexible call structures, and there are tons of birds that can mimic other birds. Maybe you just pair that ability with this deception adaptation, and it looks a bit different, but it's the same kind of trick.
OM: Do you think these behaviors are inherited, or just innate characteristics of the drongos themselves?

JO: I don't know — I'd be interested to find out. The evolutionary aspect would be that the ones who can do it get more food and are better able to survive and reproduce. Whether they learn it from their parents, it's entirely possible. We know from birds in general that they learn calls from their parents and their social groups, and there are even studies showing birds will start learning calls while they're still in the egg, listening to their parents' calls. So it's entirely possible they learn this trick socially, as far as I know.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: OM: In writing this book, what did you find is the best way to approach understanding animal behavior as it relates to human traits like lying or deception?

JO: I think there's still a little bit of baggage from old-school thinking, that you need bigger brains to be deceptive and tricky in this way, and there are still people who think it must be things like the higher apes and great apes that are capable of this stuff.

As soon as you start studying that in something like an invertebrate, it's really hard to get the idea out there — other scientists will come back and say, "No, that couldn't be possible, this must be some other type of behavior, or it just looks like tactical deception, but it's not." This happened with the researchers who did the work on cuttlefish that change one side of their body to look like a male and the other to look like a female — there was a lot of resistance to that idea, seemingly just because it was a cuttlefish, this little invertebrate, so it couldn't possibly be capable of such cleverness. But as far as the actual evidence goes, and what we can see, it's really no different from what we see in these big-brained mammals, so why not assume the same thing is going on?

paras.en: A lot of it comes down to the culture and practice of science, and the people doing the science. We're supposed to be as objective as possible, but we're still humans, we're still animals. It takes a while for ideas to change.
OM: Is there a risk that this caution has become its own kind of bias, where we assume human specialness by default until proven otherwise?

JO: Yeah, definitely. It's important, as part of scientific practice, to be as objective as possible, and as a general rule, to not anthropomorphize. But at the same time, we're just animals too — we're just another one of the great apes. We share characteristics with lots of different animals, so it's not a huge stretch to think that what's going on in our brains is also going to be similar to what's going on in other animal brains.

It's just a question of when we apply that kind of thinking, and when it's useful or not. Something similar happened in the field of understanding pain in animals — scientists studying this were always trying not to anthropomorphize, not to assume animals experienced pain the way we did. Then, the more we understood it, it became quite clear that they probably did, and it almost became an ethical question to stop with the anti-anthropomorphizing and instead go, no, we know what pain feels like, we can say that.

paras.en: We're never going to be able to see what's going on in their brains, but that doesn't excuse us from recognizing what's going on. So I think it became okay not to anthropomorphize but to recognize the similarities between humans and other animals, as opposed to always hinging on the differences between us.

OM: At the end of the chapter, you say that if you buy a scientist a few drinks, they'll eventually admit that animals can lie. I obviously can't buy you a drink over email, so I'll just ask you directly — do you think animals can lie?
JO: Yeah. I'll give a straightforward yes, because I can.

You need to get scientists out of their professional mindset, where they're trained to give the most correct answer that they can. And yes is a bit of a broad-stroke answer for a scientist when they're in professional mode, which is why you need to get them out of the lab and out to a bar or a cafe, and get them talking in human terms again.
OM: What would you say is your favorite example in the book — what are you most excited for readers to walk away with?

JO: I'll go with the cuttlefish example — the one where a male cuttlefish will put male color patterns on one side of its body and female patterns on the other, to trick other male cuttlefish. It might be my favorite because, as a young student, I worked on this particular species of cuttlefish. We were studying them, watching all of their crazy color-changing abilities, and just wondering what on earth they must be talking about, what was going on there. Then, years later, seeing the aforementioned research come out was this sort of lightbulb moment — that's what I was watching them do all along. I think that has a personal connection for me. I spent so much time looking at these creatures, being mesmerized by what they were doing, with no idea what was going on. So it was great to see scientists come in and figure it out, and answer those questions.

articles.title: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.
articles.author: James O’Hanlon

paras.en: Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.

In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?

In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.
James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.

Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.

They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.

This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.
It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.

It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.

Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.

Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.
- 'They cannot compete with the prices that fish factories will pay': How demand for fish meal takes priority over feeding people
- Photojournalist Steve Winter on his iconic Hollywood puma image, the illegal tiger trade and having a black panther knock on his door
- 'Parasites of human societies': How did we end up so close to cats?
Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.

The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.

A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.

Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.
