articles.title: Dolores Huerta, Farmworker Rights Activist Who Coined 'Sí Se Puede,' Dies at 96

paras.en: Dolores Huerta, a labor leader and civil rights activist who dedicated her life to improving working conditions for migrant farmworkers in the United States, has died at the age of 96.

Huerta died at her home in Bakersfield, California, surrounded by close family members on October 28, according to a statement released by her foundation. The cause of death was cancer, Erik Olvera, a spokesman for the family, tells the Los Angeles Times’ James Rainey.

“It’s a tough time,” Olvera adds. “She was incredibly beloved, and not only was she beloved, but she was an icon to so many people around the country and around the world, really. If anything, her family is clinging to memories and clinging to each other as they mourn.”

Born in 1930 in New Mexico, Huerta moved to Stockton, California, as a child with her mother and two brothers after her parents divorced. She graduated from Stockton High School and earned a degree from Stockton College (now San Joaquin Delta College) at a time when educational opportunities for women, especially Mexican American women, were limited.

Huerta began her career as an elementary school teacher but pivoted to advocacy after seeing farmworkers’ children coming to school hungry and barefoot. She began working for the Community Service Organization, a Latino civil rights group, where she met Cesar Chavez, who shared her commitment to improving conditions for farmworkers.

“They were only earning like 50 cents an hour,” Huerta told Good Morning America in 2020. “They had no unemployment insurance … They weren’t even able to have any kind of access to the food banks ... No bathrooms in the field, especially for the women. That was really horrible. No access to drinking water. They would actually charge them for the water that they would give the workers and of course, no rest periods, as if they were pretty much brutalized.”

In 1962, Huerta and Chavez co-founded the National Farm Workers Association, which later became the United Farm Workers. Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, the union orchestrated strikes, nonviolent protests and nationwide produce boycotts.

“The farmworkers couldn’t win by themselves,” Huerta told Smithsonian magazine’s Ryan P. Smith in 2017. “They had to reach out to the American public, and all of the 17 million Americans that decided not to eat grapes or lettuce and Gallo wine. And that’s the way that we won.”

Those efforts paved the way for the passage of the California Agricultural Labor Relations Act of 1975, which gave farmworkers the right to self-organize, form unions and engage in collective bargaining. It was the country’s first major farm-labor law outside of Hawaii, per the New York Times’ Robert D. McFadden.

The mother of 14 children, Huerta served as Chavez’s second-in-command until his death in 1993 and the union’s vice president for nearly four decades. Earlier this year, Huerta told the New York Times’ Manny Fernandez and Sarah Hurtes that Chavez had twice forced her into having sex, resulting in two pregnancies. She said she kept quiet about the sexual assaults because she didn’t want to hurt the farmworkers movement. She arranged for both girls to be raised by others but later reconnected with them.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Times investigation also found that Chavez had groomed and sexually abused girls as young as 12. Huerta said she had not been aware of Chavez’s sexual misconduct involving underage girls. “Unfortunately, he used some of his great leadership to abuse women and children—it’s really awful,” Huerta told Times.

In 2003, Huerta founded the Dolores Huerta Foundation, a social justice nonprofit, and promoted women candidates for public office as part of the Feminist Majority Foundation. She remained active into her later years, advocating for racial equality, economic justice, LGBTQ rights and women's rights.

Huerta earned numerous awards, including 15 honorary degrees and the Presidential Medal of Freedom. In 2019, California established an annual Dolores Huerta Day in recognition of her lifelong pursuit of justice.

“She made history,” Tey Marianna Nunn, associate director of content and interpretation at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Latino, tells Smithsonian magazine. “We can never forget the impact she has had on all of us.”

Huerta is credited with coining the phrase “Sí se puede,” or “yes we can,” which became a “rallying cry for workers, women, immigrants and people fighting for justice around the world,” according to the statement from her foundation. “She gave people the courage to recognize their own power—and showed them how to use it.”

articles.title: Paleontologists Discover the First Known Amphibian That Lived Entirely at Sea: a Flat, Armored Creature From 237 Million Years Ago

paras.en: Amphibians are known for straddling two worlds, dwelling on land and in water at different points in their lives. In fact, their name means “double life” in Greek. But no amphibian species has ever been known to reside exclusively in a marine environment—until now.

Two nearly complete fossilized skeletons found in southwestern China hint that an armored amphibian lived in the prehistoric salty waters there some 237 million years ago, researchers report in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution on October 26. The new species, named Gerrothorax maritimus, forces scientists to reconsider how today’s amphibians have adapted to their environments.

“This is potentially a revolutionary discovery,” says Steve Brusatte, a paleontologist at the University of Edinburgh in Scotland who wasn’t involved in the study, to Sarah Wild at Nature. “If this Triassic amphibian … really was fully marine, then it is a game-changer.” (The Triassic period stretched from 201 million to 252 million years ago.)

Out of the more than 8,000 amphibian species currently living on Earth, none are known to live in marine environments and only 2 percent have some level of salt tolerance, including the crab-eating frog. However, even this frog doesn’t do well in brackish water. That’s because amphibians have thin, permeable skin that allows them to breathe and consume water. When that skin is exposed to salt water, the animals become dehydrated.

“When a frog swims in sea water, it loses its body water because the sea water sucks out the body water through the permeable skin through osmotic pressure,” explains study co-author Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis, to Will Dunham at Reuters. “It cannot drink water either for the same reason. As a result, it loses body weight and will have to rest in freshwater to recover. This key feature prevents amphibians from becoming fully marine.”

So how could G. maritimus have accomplished a feat impossible for all amphibians today? The researchers suspect the answer lies in its unique biology and bony armor that would have prevented the animal from absorbing water through its skin. Instead, it had to drink water from its mouth, and its gills filtered out salt.
G. maritimus’ species name means “of the sea” in Latin.

G. maritimus was probably a flat, bottom-dwelling creature that sucked in prey that passed by. Multiple signs suggest the roughly 30-inch-long animal resided in the ocean. The fossils, unearthed in deep-sea sediments from Guizhou Province, China, were largely complete, suggesting the two amphibians died close to where they lived.

“Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom,” Motani explains in a statement. The species was also found next to an ancient marine reptile called an ichthyosaur. Moreover, Motani and colleagues measured the fossils’ proportions of different forms of the element strontium, a method used to date minerals and water. The proportions matched those of Late Triassic oceans, when the amphibian lived, the researchers found.

Anatomical analysis suggested that the closest relative of G. maritimus is G. pulcherrimus, an extinct amphibian that also lived during the Triassic. The two animals had similar armor and flattened bodies, although G. pulcherrimus lived in fresh water. That discovery led the researchers to conclude that G. maritimus’ marine lifestyle was an accident of evolution.
“There was a freshwater amphibian that happened to have the equipment needed to colonize the sea—the body armor,” Motani tells James Woodford at New Scientist.

Overall, the findings “reinforce the fact that the evolutionary and ecological relationships of amphibians with salt water are clearly much more complex and ancient than originally assumed,” says Gareth Hopkins, a zoologist at Western Oregon University who wasn’t involved in the study, to Nature. “At a time of rising sea levels and freshwater salinization, understanding how amphibians adapt and survive in salt water is critical to their conservation.”

articles.title: Drug-Resistant Germs Now Kill More Than 50,000 Americans Each Year, According to a New CDC Report

paras.en: Drug-resistant “superbugs” are now killing more than 50,000 Americans and infecting nearly 10 million each year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

This week, the federal health agency released its first comprehensive assessment of drug-resistant bacteria and fungi in seven years. The new report identifies 19 pathogens that currently pose a threat to human health in the United States, plus another six that are being monitored as potential threats.

Drug-resistant pathogens are those that have evolved to withstand the effects of medications designed to kill them or stop their growth, such as antibiotics, antifungals, antiparasitics and antivirals. Experts say the misuse and overuse of these treatments have contributed to the problem, along with environmental factors that seem to be helping superbugs thrive, like rising global temperatures.

When infections stop responding to standard treatments, patients may take longer to recover or end up with more severe illnesses. The risks are particularly high for people with compromised immune systems, underlying health conditions or those who use medical devices such as catheters and ventilators.

Patients in hospitals and other medical settings are also at increased risk. The CDC estimates that infections commonly associated with health care settings were responsible for more than 42,000 deaths and nearly $12 billion in health care costs in 2023.

Superbugs “prolong hospital stays, drive up health care costs and make it increasingly difficult—and sometimes impossible—for doctors to safely provide care,” Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America and an infectious-disease specialist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, says in a statement.
Did you know? A.I.-designed viruses could help with antimicrobial resistance

In August, researchers reported that they used artificial intelligence to design viruses not found in nature. The pathogens they made attack only bacteria, so the scientists propose that this technique could eventually help create treatments for antibiotic-resistant germs.

The new report classifies drug-resistant pathogens into three threat levels: urgent, serious or concerning. It also includes a watch list of potentially risky germs that researchers are still investigating to understand the threat they pose.

“The rankings are a way to differentiate the ones that we have the most lost sleep over at CDC,” says Michael Craig, who co-authored the new report and directs the CDC’s Antimicrobial Resistance Coordination and Strategy Unit, tells NBC News’ Aria Bendix. “But the thing that I always remind people is that all of these are threats.”

Four germs are listed as urgent, the highest level of threat. One is Candida auris, a fungus that spreads easily in hospitals and can cause illnesses ranging from mild skin infections to life-threatening bloodstream infections. According to the CDC, C. auris clinical cases increased by more than 50 percent between 2022 and 2023. And since 2019, the number of cases has increased nearly tenfold.

Another urgent superbug is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the bacterium that causes the sexually transmitted infection gonorrhea. It has become resistant to nearly every antibiotic used to treat it, and “it’s only a matter of time until it becomes resistant to the last available cure,” per the CDC.

The other two urgent germs are Acinetobacter and Enterobacterales, bacteria that commonly spread in health care settings. They are now resistant to even the most powerful antibiotics, including carbapenem antibiotics, so patients who develop infections have limited treatment options.

Overall, the report paints a troubling picture. But it also points to reasons for optimism. For example, the CDC has downgraded Clostridioides difficile, or “C. diff,” a bacterium that can cause diarrhea and colon inflammation. Cases are declining, dropping from 455,560 in 2018 to 412,504 in 2023, likely due to better diagnosis and infection prevention and treatment efforts.
The new report “shows both the progress we’ve made and the significant work that remains,” Erica Schwartz, director of the CDC, says in a statement.

The CDC last issued a report on drug-resistant bacteria and fungi in 2019. However, the agency cautioned against comparing numbers from the two assessments because it used different data sources and methods this time around. Moving forward, the CDC plans to release an update every two years, per NBC News.

Beyond the U.S., superbugs are a growing threat to public health around the world. Research suggests that antibiotic-resistant infections could result in more than 39 million deaths by 2050. Researchers are racing to develop new drugs that could help address the problem, but experts worry that these efforts may not keep pace with the growing threat.

“The scientific community has developed and approved new antibiotics in recent years,” said Yvan Hutin, previously the director of antimicrobial resistance at the World Health Organization, in a statement earlier this year. “This is good, but unfortunately not sufficient to catch up with evolving drug-resistant bacteria, especially against those of greatest concern. We need a reliable pipeline with new antibacterial agents that are innovative, affordable, accessible to all those who need them.”

articles.title: An AI Agent Injected Drugs Into a Live Mouse’s Brain
articles.author: Emily Mullin

paras.en: If you give an AI agent a robotic arm, an injector, and a live mouse, it might just perform brain surgery.

Biotech founder Gabriel Ocana Santero recently did that using an agent to successfully carry out a brain injection procedure on a living mouse. Though it required some extra steps, it offers a glimpse into how AI could eventually become an active participant in laboratory research.

Santero posted about the experiment on social media and tells WIRED he was interested in exploring what happens when AI agents are given direct access to lab equipment, rather than simply being asked to design experiments or analyze results.

“We’ve realized that we need to connect these agents to a lab to get the maximum value from them,” he says. Santero is the CEO and cofounder of Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco–based startup using AI to analyze brain activity to develop drugs for epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases.

AI models are trained primarily on published scientific literature. That means they may miss important information about the research process, including failed experiments, unexpected observations, and decisions scientists make in real time. Integrating AI models with real-world experiments can make the models more reliable, Santero says.

It’s why his team decided to connect an AI agent to a custom-built surgical setup used for performing brain injections on mice. The rig included a motorized device used to immobilize a mouse and a camera that allowed the agent to observe the procedure, move an injection needle, and control the delivery of a compound. For the experiment, his team was testing a gene therapy to see whether it could reduce seizures in a mouse with epilepsy.

They asked the AI model to choose a treatment from 19 options in a spreadsheet. A veterinary surgeon first performed a craniotomy on the mouse while the AI agent observed. The agent selected the therapy, brain region, and injection coordinates, then controlled the robotic arms and injector needle, as well as all the parameters, such as volume and speed.

The team initially tested Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 model, but it refused to guide the needle into the mouse’s brain, suggesting it might stop midway through the surgery, which could endanger the animal.

“He did the experimental planning, but when it was time to inject, he said, ‘something on my output is telling me I shouldn't do this,’” Santero says, referring to the agent. “That was very interesting.”

The team switched to using Claude Sonnet 5, which agreed to proceed. Opus is a heavy-reasoning intelligence specialist best for complex multistep problem-solving, according to Anthropic, while Sonnet is better suited for everyday tasks, though it may be a stretch to call mouse brain surgery a common chore. (Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.)

Frontier labs have been planning for more widespread physical manifestations of AI, and researchers have already begun enlisting agents to do other things in the physical world. In August, Anthropic put out a framework for how its models can interact with the real world. More recently, AI engineers put GPT, Claude, and Grok in charge of a car to pick up lunch at In-N-Out Burger. Only one of the models succeeded.

The brain injection procedure wasn’t without hiccups either. The researchers had established safeguards, including requiring the AI to propose an injection plan for human approval and installing an emergency button a human could hit that would disconnect the rig’s motors. They also restricted the agent's access to the underlying equipment code to prevent it from modifying its own operating rules.

However, a technical glitch disrupted the equipment's coordinate system. Although the agent correctly recognized that the calculated injection position was wrong, it refused to modify the code to correct the problem because its instructions explicitly prohibited doing so.

The team resolved the issue by using a separate AI agent on Opus 5 to make the necessary code changes, but they didn’t tell the agent that a live surgery was happening. The resulting back and forth delayed the procedure, Santero says: A typical brain injection surgery like this takes about 45 minutes, while this experiment lasted slightly longer than an hour. They’re now waiting for the therapy to take effect before assessing its impact on seizures.

Despite those glitches, Santero and his team were impressed by the agent’s performance. They’re testing Grok and other models next to figure out whether one model performs better. The company is also experimenting with agent-controlled craniotomies—a much more complicated task—but wants to be absolutely sure of their safety before moving to live surgeries.
“A mistake at that stage could seriously harm the mouse,” he says.

Santero thinks AI agents will increasingly work alongside human scientists, with direct access to lab equipment. For now, he says human oversight is key, particularly when experiments involve living animals. And it’s far too soon to unleash an AI agent on a human brain.
As for the mouse, Santero reports it’s recovering well.

articles.title: Meta’s Muse Could Upend All Kinds of Businesses. It Hasn’t Yet
articles.author: Paresh Dave

paras.en: Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks, is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average.

Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents.

Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.”

While financial experts have suspected that users may ask Muse to dump unused subscriptions and memberships, fitness chain Life Time Group said it has “seen zero” cancellations from agents. Public Storage and Hartford Insurance Group offered similar data. In India, the delivery app giant Eternal estimated agentic commerce as “close to zero.”

The comments leave questions about where users of Muse, Instinct, and other popular AI agents are spending their money. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on his company’s earnings call this month that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. Over 25 percent used it for shopping, more than any other task and above the company’s expectations, he added.

Meta declined to comment beyond the earnings call remarks, but pointed to partnerships with 10 retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of them last reported earnings before Muse launched and haven’t shared data about it yet.
Across the board, executives acknowledged agents are at an early stage. But immense public anxiety about AI technologies has left companies searching for any lessons they can from the outset.

Despite the seemingly slow uptake, some are already hard at work optimizing their websites for agents. Chipotle chief digital officer Arlie Sisson told reporters this week that the restaurant chain discovered agents struggling to complete purchases because of hiccups from applying loyalty discounts or ordering after-hours. Muse’s debut increased agentic orders by a single-digit percentage, she said. So Chipotle is now tidying up its website code to help agents better navigate and satisfy the hungry humans behind them.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Similar discussions are underway at Doordash, even though CEO and Meta board member Tony Xu said present hype about agents might be “delusional.” Costco and Extra Space Storage said sales originating from AI chatbots such as Gemini and ChatGPT are surging as the companies optimize their online content for the tools, so they plan to do the same for AI agents.

Reliance on agents could be costly. Zuckerberg said Meta plans to charge businesses a fee for transactions facilitated by Muse, and he predicted that this source of revenue would eventually top the company’s massive advertising business. InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf is taking a cautious approach in ongoing talks with Meta. “We haven't come to any conclusions on what an eventual collaboration could look like, if any,” he said.

Security issues and errant orders remain top of mind. This week, Bank of America became the latest big bank to warn customers about giving login information to AI assistants. “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access,” chief client care officer Ashley Ross wrote in an email.

There’s also the possibility that agents encourage comparison shopping in a way that hurts profits. Executives at many companies dismissed the notion. They suggested product quality, customer service, and brand trust would still factor into purchase decisions despite less human involvement.

Stances on agents are evolving quickly. Amazon blocked Muse last month, contending that users would prefer its own Alexa shopping agent. But this week the retail giant acknowledged that it anticipates working with outside agents. Insurance marketplace Insurify also blocked Muse but this week changed its mind after introducing technology to ensure agents could present accurate offers.

articles.title: Backup by Biolite Review: A Cool Idea
articles.author: Christopher Null

paras.en: Every part of a power outage is always a massive nuisance, but nothing is quite as aggravating as losing power to your refrigerator and the resultant spoilage of everything inside it.

Homes with a whole-house battery backup can avoid this headache, but the cost for a system like a Tesla Powerwall can easily hit $15,000 after installation. It takes an awful lot of melted ice cream for those numbers to balance out.

BioLite—known for its range of lighting and portable power solutions—is on the cusp of launching an alternative to whole-house batteries. Backup by BioLite is a modular battery system designed specifically with the fridge in mind, offering long-term emergency power at a fraction of the cost of more complex systems and which homeowners can install themselves. I installed it in my home and found it a capable (if limited) way to get a little extra peace of mind.

Backup by BioLite is hardly a difficult concept to grasp. The massive battery—offering 1526 watt-hours of power with a rated output of 1800 watts (and supporting peak surges up to 3000 watts)—mounts on the wall behind your refrigerator, or it can simply sit on top of it. The power pack measures 29 inches high by 13 inches wide, and a single unit weighs a hefty 40 pounds. No special wiring is required. You simply plug the Backup into a standard 120-volt outlet, then plug your refrigerator into the Backup.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Want more power? Backup’s Core unit can be daisy-chained to a Backup Extend add-on device, an identically sized (but slightly lighter) unit that doubles the power capacity to 3072 Wh.

Depending on your refrigerator, the full “Backup Complete” solution, with two cells, can provide up to 60 hours of running time if the grid goes down. If that’s not enough, additional Backup Extend devices can be added in series, with a total maximum capacity of 10.5 KWh. (Though, at that point, you may as well spring for a whole-house solution.)

One of the biggest selling points of Backup by BioLite is that you can install it yourself, with no electrician. I’ve got no trouble wielding a drill, so I undertook the effort to see if BioLite’s promise of a 30-minute install would pan out. I tested Backup Complete, with two Backup batteries situated side by side.

The process seems straightforward (and is enhanced by a helpful printed manual), but I quickly learned that my refrigerator’s location—tucked into an alcove—would complicate things because of the limited space in which to work. BioLite suggests having an extra pair of hands to hoist the heavy battery packs into place, but there was simply no room for my wife to squeeze into the alcove to help with any of the process. I managed on my own, but I expect this will present a challenge for some.

articles.title: California woman accused of deliberately running over 9-week-old puppy

paras.en: Oct. 31 (UPI) -- A 75-year-old woman in California faces federal charges after allegedly luring a 9-week-old puppy beneath her minivan with food and running over the animal, killing it, prosecutors said Friday.
Hanh Minh Nguyen, of Anaheim, was charged Thursday with animal crushing, a federal felony punishable by up to seven years in prison.
Prosecutors said investigators obtained surveillance video showing a woman releasing a black-and-white pit bull puppy from a Honda Odyssey minivan in September.
The video allegedly shows the woman dropping food near the driver's door and gesturing for the puppy to approach.
As the vehicle moved forward, its rear tire ran over the animal.
Prosecutors said the driver stopped with the vehicle resting on the puppy for about 15 seconds before leaving.
An examination of the animal's remains found that it died from a crushed skull and suffered severe pain for several minutes before its death.
Police identified Nguyen as the suspected driver and arrested her Oct. 1.
She also faces animal cruelty charges in Orange County Superior Court.

articles.title: Former Army contractor charged with leaking military information

paras.en: Oct. 31 (UPI) -- A former U.S. government contractor was arrested after allegedly sharing classified military information on social media and stealing night-vision equipment from an Army Special Operations facility, officials said Friday.
James Thomas Ashbacher, 37 of Spring Lake, N.C., was arrested Tuesday by the FBI following a federal indictment accusing him of unlawfully transmitting and keeping national defense information.
He also faces a charge of stealing government property.
Prosecutors said Ashbacher began working in 2021 for a private company that provided security and emergency management services at Fort Bragg.
His position gave him access to classified military information through a top-secret security clearance.
Investigators said Ashbacher photographed and copied material depicting classified military operations without authorization.
He allegedly uploaded the images and videos to a social media platform, where other users later shared them on another site.
A search of his home uncovered an award document containing classified defense information, investigators said.
Agents also recovered a night-vision system belonging to an Army Special Operations unit that had previously been reported missing.

articles.title: Calif. Botox doctor gets 15 years for $45 million Medicare fraud

paras.en: Oct. 31 (UPI) -- A California doctor who fraudulently billed Medicare $45 million for Botox injections while she was vacationing in Mexico and other destinations was sentenced to 15 years in prison, officials said Friday.
Violetta Mailyan, 45 of Glendale, was sentenced Thursday for defrauding Medicare through her medical practice, Healthy Way Medical Center.
Prosecutors said Mailyan submitted more than $45 million in fraudulent claims for Botox treatments that were unnecessary, performed for cosmetic reasons or never administered.
Medicare covers Botox injections for certain medical conditions, including chronic migraines, but does not generally pay for cosmetic procedures.
Investigators found that Mailyan billed Medicare for thousands of treatments supposedly performed on days when her clinic was closed. Those claims totaled more than $19 million.
Prosecutors said she also submitted claims for treatments in California while traveling in Mexico, Hawaii, Las Vegas, Pennsylvania and New York.
During one trip to Cabo San Lucas, Mexico, Mailyan billed Medicare more than $200,000 for services she supposedly provided while away.
Mailyan attempted to conceal the fraud by creating false medical records and forging patient signatures after learning she was under investigation.
One of the patients she claimed to have treated was serving time in federal prison when the supposed appointment took place.
Prosecutors said Mailyan spent proceeds from the scheme on luxury purchases, including two Tesla vehicles, a Cybertruck and five properties in California.
Her purchases also included a 17th-century crossbow valued at $12,000 and a $3,000 painting.
A federal jury convicted Mailyan in May on nine counts of wire fraud and three counts of obstructing a healthcare fraud investigation.
The court ordered her to pay more than $32.9 million in restitution to Medicare.
She must also surrender more than $16 million in assets seized by federal authorities, including real estate, investments and bank funds.

articles.title: ‘SNL’ Parodies Nicki Minaj After Her Trump Rally Appearance
articles.author: Jessica Lynch

paras.en: Saturday Night Live turned its Halloween cold open on Saturday (Oct. 31) into a send-up of Nicki Minaj’s support for President Donald Trump, a week after the rapper joined him on the campaign trail.

Cast member Saidah Belo-Osagie played Minaj, bursting into the sketch near its end as James Austin Johnson’s Trump praised her loyalty to his movement. “Trump’s out here killing it,” Belo-Osagie’s Minaj declared, “and by it, I mean my career.” The sketch also cast her as Trump’s next choice for White House press secretary.

The parody drew directly on Minaj’s appearance at Trump’s Oct. 25 rally in Port Huron, Michigan, where she traveled with him on Air Force One and backed Republican candidates Mike Rogers and John James ahead of Tuesday’s (Nov. 3) midterm elections. During the rally, Trump invited Minaj to stand before the crowd and commented on her appearance, a moment the sketch played on with Johnson’s Trump making a string of jokes about the subject.

The press secretary gag also had a real-world source. A Trump staffer floated Minaj for the role during the Air Force One trip, and Trump later told The Benny Show it was “a good idea,” adding, “I’m gonna think about that.” Minaj has also said she is “not going anywhere” after Trump called her his “favorite.”

The cold open was framed as a ride through a budget Halloween haunted attraction, with Grace Reiter and Jeremy Culhane as a couple on a date and Kenan Thompson as a Grim Reaper guide. Tom Hanks then appeared as David S. Pumpkins, the oddball character he introduced on the show in 2016, backed by his dancing skeleton sidekicks Mikey Day and former cast member Bobby Moynihan, in what the sketch itself called the character’s third outing.

Before the bit could get going, Johnson’s Trump froze the scene and cut it short. “I’ll save you four minutes: he keeps popping up and confusing people on the ride. The end,” he told the audience, before comparing himself to Pumpkins: “We both appeared in 2016, we’re both very loud, very orange.” He went on to complain about Republican polling ahead of the midterms before Belo-Osagie’s Minaj made her entrance.
Minaj has not publicly addressed the sketch.

The rapper remains one of the most successful acts in Billboard chart history. In 2018, she became the first woman to log 100 entries on the Billboard Hot 100, and she holds the most Hot 100 top 10s among female rappers. In 2020, she and Doja Cat became the first female rap duo to top the Hot 100, with the remix of “Say So.”

Obsession star Inde Navarrette hosted the episode, her first time in the role. Gracie Abrams was the musical guest, her second SNL appearance after her December 2024 debut. She arrived fresh off the release of her new single “Here You Come, There You Go” on Oct. 29, and ahead of her Look at My Life arena tour, which launches Dec. 2 in Denver in support of her third album, Daughter From Hell.
SNL airs live on Saturday (Oct. 31), with a start time of 11:30 p.m. ET/PT.

articles.title: Tovah Feldshuh Shuts Down ‘Nobody Wants This’ Cast Tension Rumors Amid Adam Brody “Free Palestine” Support
articles.author: McKinley Franklin

paras.en: Nobody Wants This actress Tovah Feldshuh is shutting down claims that tensions are rising among the cast amid recent comments Adam Brody made saying he is in support of “a free Palestine.”

“Tensions are NOT RISING. Profound differences of opinion are. Please do not conflate the two — And none of it will be brought to the set,” she wrote in response to a Threads post made by AzatTV that reads, “Tensions are emerging on the set of the Netflix series Nobody Wants This.”
Feldshuh added, “I deeply enjoy filming [Nobody Wants This] and hope we are chosen to go on for a fourth season.”

In an interview with GQ, Brody said of the war in Gaza, “put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine.” He added, “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”

Feldshuh, who plays the mother of Brody’s character Noah on the Netflix show, told The New York Post of the actor’s comments, “To accuse the Jewish people of genocide is wild.” She added, “It’s right out of Hitler’s playbook. You take the victim and you make the victim the perpetrator.”
The actress said that it “makes a difference to the [Jewish] community,” when asked by the Post if “accusations of genocide are worse when they come from Jewish people themselves.”

“I believe that the perseverance of the existence of the state of Israel is crucial to the well-being of the democratic world and of the free world,” Feldshuh said. “Of course, Israel needs the United States, [but] the United States needs Israel, believe you me.”
Feldshuh also told the outlet, “My job, as Bina but also as Tovah, is to love the people on set at my place of work, to be kind.”
She added, “With the backdrop of global antisemitism, I am thrilled to be chosen to play a Jewish matriarch. Thrilled and proud, and that will never change.”
Erin Foster, creator of Nobody Wants This, has also reacted to Brody’s statement, saying on the Not Skinny But Not Fat podcast that “it’s complicated.”

“I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing,” Foster said. “While I love Adam, I also disagree with him, and that’s okay.”

“I think that as the creator of the show, all I can say is that I want our Jewish fans to know that I see you and I hear you and I understand how you feel,” she continued. “And the show has always been and always will be a love letter to Judaism. That is why I made this show. It’s because of how beautiful of an experience I’ve had becoming Jewish and being a Jewish person, and sitting here right now at this time in the world where there is almost zero positive representation of Jewish people, I think it’s so important to have that.”

articles.title: Heidi Klum Reveals This Year’s (Very Bloody) Halloween Costume
articles.author: Kirsten Chuba

paras.en: It wouldn’t be Halloween without Heidi Klum, as the star revealed yet another jaw-dropping costume at her signature party on Saturday night.
The Queen of Halloween, as she has become known, celebrated the 25th anniversary of her NYC Halloween party this year, and Klum took it to the next level as she showed up as a severed hand.

She arrived in a truck covered in red “danger” sings, helped to the ground by actors in yellow hazmat suits. Klum’s elaborate costume includes a bloody wrist and her head at the center of the hand, with fingers featuring rings and a fresh manicure; she revealed in red carpet interviews it was an intricate recreation of her own hand. The star appeared without husband Tom Kaulitz, who has dressed up alongside her in recent years.

Klum is hosting the event, presented by Apothic and Butterfinger, at Cathédrale Restaurant at Moxy East Village. The party has become one of Spooky Season’s most iconic events, as Klum always turns up in an elaborate look — in recent years, she’s transformed into Medusa, E.T., a peacock, Fiona from Shrek, Jessica Rabbit and famously, a worm.

The supermodel has been teasing glimpses at her costume on her Instagram, teasing her transformation all day long while asking her followers to submit their guesses on what she would become. Klum collaborates on her costumes with special effects makeup designer Mike Marino, who won an Emmy for his work on The Penguin. Marino revealed in a recent interview that “this costume this year is one of the most elaborate costumes ever made. It’s so difficult to do and just the complication of it is really challenging.”
