articles.title: Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists

paras.en: Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists

- A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmosâs deepest mysteries.

Scientists have proposed a surprising new explanation for why the universe exists, and it centers on a mysterious particle that physicists have largely overlooked for decades. Their theory suggests this forgotten particle may have played a crucial role in shaping the early cosmos and allowing matter to survive after the Big Bang.

The research addresses one of the most fundamental mysteries in physics: why does the universe contain matter instead of nothing at all? Scientists believe matter and antimatter were produced in nearly equal amounts in the early universe. When these opposites encounter one another, they annihilate and release energy. If they had existed in perfectly equal quantities, virtually all matter could have disappeared, leaving no material to form stars, planets, or life.

Now, researchers from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur believe they may have found an important piece of the puzzle. Their explanation involves a little-understood relative of the neutrino, an extremely lightweight particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.
A Forgotten Particle With a Powerful Role in the Early Universe

The team focused on a type of particle known as a 'decoupled' heavy neutrino. Unlike ordinary neutrinos, this hypothetical heavier relative has generally been considered too weakly connected to other particles to significantly influence the universe.

However, the researchers found that its unusually long lifetime could have made it far more important than previously thought. According to their calculations, the particle may have survived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe's energy density as the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang.
That brief period of dominance could have altered how the early universe evolved, influencing the conditions that ultimately allowed matter to outnumber antimatter.
Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton, an author of the study, explained:
"This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.

"However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period."
The findings were published in Physical Review Letters, a scientific journal of the American Physical Society.
How a Heavy Neutrino Could Explain Why Matter Survived

Previous attempts to explain why matter prevailed over antimatter generally left out the decoupled heavy neutrino. Because it interacts so weakly with other particles, scientists assumed it would have little influence on the processes responsible for creating the imbalance.

The new research challenges that assumption. The team found that even a particle with extremely weak interactions could indirectly affect the conditions under which matter gained its crucial advantage.

This imbalance, known as matter and antimatter asymmetry, is essential to understanding our existence. For reasons physicists are still trying to explain, the early universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter. That small difference allowed some matter to remain after most particles and their antiparticles annihilated one another.
"The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred," added Dr. Roshan.

"The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles - like electrons and other leptons - interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.
"This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up."

The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle associated with the mechanism that gives many elementary particles their mass. In the researchers' proposed scenario, the heavy neutrino changed the temperature conditions governing important particle interactions involving the Higgs boson.

By shifting when these interactions occurred, the particle could have influenced how the imbalance between matter and antimatter developed. In other words, something long considered insignificant may have helped determine why the universe contains matter at all.
Ancient Gravitational Waves Could Reveal the Answer
The theory could also have important implications for understanding how the universe expanded in its earliest stages.

Study co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings suggest that the forgotten particle may have dramatically altered the expansion history of the young cosmos.
He added: "It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.
"The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.
"These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang."

Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space and time. Scientists believe processes in the extremely early universe may have generated primordial gravitational waves that carry information about conditions from that distant era.

According to the new theory, the temporary dominance of the heavy neutrino could have left recognizable signatures in those ancient signals. Detecting such patterns could eventually provide a way to investigate whether the proposed particle really influenced the universe's earliest evolution.

For now, the explanation remains theoretical. But it offers physicists a new possibility for solving one of cosmology's deepest mysteries: how matter survived when its encounter with antimatter could have left the universe almost entirely empty.
Materials provided by University of Southampton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Halloween night sky 2026 — Saturn, shooting stars and a space station await US stargazers
articles.author: Joe Rao

paras.en: There could be more than just ghosts and ghouls lurking in the skies this Halloween! From Saturn's spectacular rings to shooting stars and even a space station flyover, the night sky has a few treats of its own in store for U.S. skywatchers on Oct. 31.

Based on the latest national forecast, skies will be mainly clear on Saturday evening over most of New York State, northeast Pennsylvania, northern New Jersey and New England as well as a swath of the southern and central Great Plains, central Rockies, a portion of the Pacific Northwest and central and south Florida, as costumed kids arrive at the door looking for candy or some other Halloween treat.

Temperatures will be mostly in the chilly 40s across the Northeast US, upper 50s and 60s for the nation's midsection, warm 70s to near 80 for the southern US, including Florida and the Gulf Coast, and 40s for much of the western US. Unfortunately, a storm moving across the nation's heartland may spell rainy skies for parts of Iowa and Nebraska, south to the Gulf Coast.

For those blessed with a generally fair evening, there will be views of mid-autumn stars and constellations plus a bright planet shining prominently in the early evening sky. If you plan to accompany children around your neighborhood, you might want to enlighten them by pointing out some of those objects that will be visible in the sky. Better yet, if you have a telescope, give your visitors a treat of a different kind: Give them a close-up view of some of those celestial sights.
At the top of the viewing list: The lord of the rings

At around 7 p.m. local time, tell your young audience to make a clenched fist with their hands and then hold them out at arm's length. Now, tell them to go "two fists" up from the east-southeast horizon and they will see a bright star, shining with a yellow-white hue. Now, direct your telescope toward that "star" and when you gaze through the eyepiece, you will not be looking at a star at all . . . but a planet!

This sixth planet out from the sun, just might be the most beautiful of all. Its rings are still readily evident, although currently they appear somewhat edge-on with the south face tilted only about 6 and a half degrees to our line of sight. A telescope magnifying 30-power will bring them out; they appear to bisect the ball of the planet. While this is far from their appearance compared to other years, the view should still look impressive to those who have never seen the ringed planet for themselves.

paras.en: Because they are active over Halloween, the Taurid meteor shower is sometimes called the "Halloween Fireballs." The bits of debris that make up the Taurids are a little larger than average, so they can result in brighter meteors and even fireballs, or exploding meteors (called bolides), that streak across the sky and leave incandescent trains in their wake. While they are most active during the second week of November, a few forerunners can show up on Halloween night, darting from out of the east-northeast part of the sky. So, if you or your young visitors see something resembling a flare from a Roman candle sweeping majestically across the evening sky, it may very well be a Taurid meteor.

paras.en: And for those in the Northeast U.S., a space station!

Not the International Space Station, but the Tianhe-1 core module, the first module to launch of the Tiangong space station. It was launched into orbit on 29 April 2021, as the first launch of the final phase of the Tiangong program, part of the China Manned Space Program (Project 921). On Halloween evening, Tianhe-1 will be following a track from Chicago to New York at an altitude of 240 miles (385 km) and should be readily visible to the naked eye across the Northeast US within a few minutes of 7 p.m. EDT, wherever skies are reasonably clear.

paras.en: The Tiangong Space Station should appear to resemble a very bright star moving across the sky on a general west-to-east course. For places near and along the flight path, the Space Station will appear to pass almost directly overhead. For those situated south of the track, Tiangong will reach its highest point above the northern horizon; those situated north of the track will see the station peak high in the south.

If you see it, tell your young viewers that three astronauts are currently living and working aboard the Tiangong Space Station, of which the Tianhe core module serves as the main living quarters. If you would like specific details on when and where to see the Space Station from your hometown, check out Heavens-Above, a non-profit website and mobile application that tracks satellites, the International Space Station (ISS), comets, and astronomical events in real time.

Another website that provides live information, including an orbit map on Tianhe-1, is NY2O.com. Check its menu list on the right side of the page and look for the blue box: "10-Day Predictions for CSS (Tianhe-1)."
Helpful hints for young telescope viewers
In the September 2019 issue of The Astronomical League Magazine "Reflector," author Richard W. Schmude Jr., offered some tips for those who plan to do public outreach for astronomy on Halloween:

"Firstly, children sometimes grab or touch the eyepiece, so use an inexpensive one. I gently warn children not to touch the telescope. In my area, parents have learned to tell their children not to touch the telescope. In some cases, a child will grab the eyepiece, causing the telescope to shift. For this reason, a Dobsonian telescope with a good finderscope is a good choice for Halloween outreach. A small stool or booster ladder may help very small viewers. Sometimes, parents hold their children up to look through the eyepiece. One may also place a monitor-connected video camera in the telescope and people can easily see the object on a screen." "Finally," adds Mr. Schmude, "I have my bag of goodies next to my telescope so that the children get two treats!"

paras.en: Whatever your weather, Happy Halloween from all of us at Space.com!

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

Joe Rao is Space.com's skywatching columnist, as well as a veteran meteorologist and eclipse chaser who also serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky & Telescope and other publications. Joe is an 8-time Emmy-nominated meteorologist who served the Putnam Valley region of New York for over 21 years. You can find him on Twitter and YouTube tracking lunar and solar eclipses, meteor showers and more. To find out Joe's latest project, visit him on Twitter.

articles.title: Betelgeuse is haunted by a cosmic poltergeist tormenting the doomed star's atmosphere
articles.author: Sharmila Kuthunur

paras.en: Something spooky is stirring in the shadows of the infamous star Betelgeuse, a cosmic poltergeist that is disrupting the atmosphere of the red supergiant.

New radio observations have shown Betelgeuse's smaller stellar companion, Siwarha (not Betelguese Betelguese, unfortunately), cutting through the supergiant's extended atmosphere and leaving a wake in its path, like a jet boat slicing through a lake.

Because the name of this red supergiant star located about 650 light-years away from Earth, marking the shoulder of constellation Orion, is Betelgeuse, which means "the hand of al-Jawza" in Arabic, the companion was named Siwarha, meaning "her bracelet."

"This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere," Lynn Matthews, the principal research scientist at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Haystack Observatory who led the new observations, said in a statement.

Using data collected from 2021 to 2026 using the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array in New Mexico and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile, Matthews and colleagues found that Betelgeuse's atmosphere stretches into an egg shape when the companion star is farthest away and rounds out when the companion passes in front of or behind it.

The same data also showed that Betelgeuse itself has largely recovered from the "Great Dimming" that made headlines in 2020. This recovery comes after the red supergiant "sneezed" in 2020, dramatically ejecting tons of gas and dust and fading to its dimmest in more than a century.

Among the long-standing mysteries of Betelgeuse, scientists have puzzled over a brightening and dimming cycle that lasts roughly 2,100 days. Recent studies pointed to a low-mass companion orbiting deep inside the star's atmosphere, and its existence was confirmed in early 2026.

Though Siwarha itself is too faint to detect directly at radio wavelengths, its influence shows up in the star's shape, the new study found. To confirm the effect, the researchers say, they will need to observe more of the companion's orbit, especially at radio frequencies that have so far been sparsely sampled.

The Next Generation Very Large Array, a planned telescope, should make this kind of monitoring far more routine, according to the team. With sharper vision, researchers could see how red supergiants like Betelgeuse shed their material as they near the end of their lives, and how a close companion might affect that process by tugging on that ejected matter.
This research is described in a paper published in The Astronomical Journal.

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

articles.title: The moon, Mars, and Jupiter shine in the heart of the Lion overnight on Nov. 1-2
articles.author: Anthony Wood

paras.en: The moon dives towards the glowing heart of the constellation Leo for a spectacular rendezvous with Mars and Jupiter overnight on Nov. 1-2, as the glittering stars of the Beehive Cluster shine nearby. Here's what you need to know.

Look to the eastern horizon an hour after midnight to see the 45%-lit waning moon shining less than 5 degrees from the red light of Mars — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length to the night sky.

Jupiter's bright light will gleam just below the red planet, with the bright star Regulus lining up beyond to form a dazzling procession leading back to the horizon. The stars of the Beehive Cluster (M44) can be found twinkling 10 degrees from the unlit side of the lunar disk around this time, in the middle of the constellation Cancer.

Stargazers in Australia, Indonesia and a host of other island nations and territories will see the moon pass directly in front of Jupiter, hiding its light in an event known as an occultation starting at 3:45 p.m. EST (2045 GMT) on Nov. 2 , according to In-The-Sky.org. However, the exact visibility and timings depend on location.

The cosmic pile-up serves as a spectacular reminder of the scale and diversity of targets on display in the night sky. After all, the moon appears largest from our Earthly perspective, but in reality it's less than half the diameter of Mars.

Jupiter, meanwhile, is over 20 times wider than the red planet, while mighty Regulus is up to four times larger than the sun, andcould easily fit all the planets of the solar system in its vast expanse.

By moonrise on the night of Nov. 3, the lunar crescent will have leapt past Jupiter and Mars, to appear just 1 degree from the blue-white light of Regulus for viewers in the U.S. Meanwhile, viewers in several South American countries including Brazil, Peru, Argentina and Bolivia will see the moon occult Regulus beginning at 6:59 EST (1024 GMT) on Nov. 3. The exact timings for a selection of South American countries can be found below, courtesy of In-The-Sky.org.

Want to get a closer look at the moon and planets of the solar system? Then be sure to check out our picks of the best telescopes and binoculars for exploring the night sky, including the Celestron NexStar 8SE, which we rank as the best motorized telescope out there.
Editor's Note: If you would like to share your astrophotography with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

articles.title: Global Satcom Services Revenues to Reach $145 Billion by 2035
articles.author: Novaspace

paras.en: Paris, France | October 2026 – Global satellite services revenues are forecast to grow 44% to reach $145 billion by 2035, according to the 33rd edition of Novaspace’s Satellite Connectivity and Video Market report. The next decade will mark a fundamental shift in the industry as data services become the dominant growth engine, driving revenues to nearly $100 billion by 2035.

Data services are expected to increase their share of total satellite services revenues from 26% to 68% over the decade, as demand for connectivity accelerates across consumer, defense, government, and enterprise markets.

While video remains the industry’s largest revenue segment today, future growth will be driven by connectivity. Consumer Broadband, Milsatcom, and Enterprise Networks are forecast to lead market expansion, adding $22.6 billion, $19.2 billion, and $17.2 billion in revenues, respectively, over the next decade.

Milsatcom is emerging as a particularly important growth engine, fueled by rising defense spending and broader adoption of satcom-enabled operational concepts across military forces. At the same time, NGSO constellations are becoming an increasingly important source of resilient capacity for government and defense users.

“Satellite connectivity is moving firmly into the mainstream,” said Dimitri Buchs, Project Manager and Editor of the report. “The rapid expansion of NGSO capacity, declining bandwidth costs, and growing demand for resilient, always-available connectivity are fundamentally changing where and how satellite communications compete.”

The satellite capacity market is forecast to exceed $46 billion by 2035, more than tripling from 2025 levels. Video Distribution, the largest capacity segment in 2025, is expected to account for just 3% of capacity revenues by 2035. Consumer Broadband and Milsatcom, meanwhile, are projected to represent more than half of total capacity revenues.

Declining bandwidth costs, driven by HTS systems and a growing number of NGSO projects, are accelerating satellite connectivity’s expansion into mass-market applications. Providers such as Starlink are increasingly competing with terrestrial broadband on price, strengthening satellite broadband’s position as a viable alternative to fiber and wireless connectivity in a growing range of markets.

The transformation is also reshaping the role of GEO operators. Following a low of six commercial GEO orders in 2024, the market rebounded to 10 orders in 2025, with another 14 recorded by mid-September 2026. The renewed activity reflects evolving multi-orbit strategies and continued demand for GEO capabilities alongside rapidly expanding NGSO systems.

“This is not a return to the traditional GEO model,” Buchs added. “Software-defined satellites, more flexible commercial models, sovereign requirements, and growing multi-orbit strategies are redefining GEO’s role. The future of satellite communications will not be GEO or NGSO—it will increasingly be an ecosystem in which each architecture serves distinct and complementary requirements.”

The 33rd edition of Satellite Connectivity and Video Market provides a comprehensive assessment of global satellite service revenues, capacity demand, pricing trends, competitive dynamics, and operator strategies across video, broadband, enterprise, mobility, government, and defense markets through 2035.

This edition introduces a granular bottom-up model for Enterprise Networks Back-up terminals, providing greater visibility into market demand and deployment trends. It also features a revised commercial Milsatcom model with deeper analysis by region, frequency band, and infrastructure type.

The report also provides an updated assessment of major developments shaping the satellite communications market, including the evolution of NGSO constellations, emerging Q/V frequency bands and other regulatory developments, government and defense spending trends, and the changing competitive dynamics between satellite and terrestrial connectivity.

articles.title: Ukrainian startup, GomSpace test satellite for future communications network
articles.author: Sandra Erwin

paras.en: WASHINGTON — A Ukrainian defense technology company and a Danish satellite manufacturer have begun operating an experimental communications satellite in orbit.

Ukrainian startup Himera and Denmark’s GomSpace said Oct. 27 that their Obria Nano satellite, launched Oct. 1 aboard the SpaceX Transporter-18 rideshare mission, is undergoing tests. The companies plan to design a constellation that would provide communications coverage across Ukraine.

The project is one of at least two European-backed initiatives aimed at giving Ukraine greater control over satellite communications, following disruptions this month to SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield services that affected Ukrainian military operations.

The announcement comes five days after Finnish satellite manufacturer Iceye and telecommunications equipment maker Nokia signed a letter of intent with Ukraine’s Defense Ministry to explore developing a sovereign broadband satellite communications network.

Ukraine has relied heavily on SpaceX’s satellite services for battlefield communications since Russia’s invasion in 2022. The services have become essential to military command networks, drone operations and communications in areas where terrestrial infrastructure has been destroyed or disrupted.
But restrictions imposed in mid-October limited satellite connectivity, interfering with Ukrainian drone operations, including efforts to intercept Russian attack drones.

Ukraine said Oct. 24 that Starlink and Starshield services had returned to normal operating speeds. The disruptions prompted a dispute over responsibility, with SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk and U.S. officials offering conflicting explanations about who had authorized the limits.

Himera and GomSpace said the Obria Nano project is intended to establish a communications system under Ukrainian control, with plans eventually to manufacture satellites and ground terminals domestically.

“For us, this project is about more than launching a satellite. It is an opportunity to lay the foundation for an independent communications network for Ukraine,” said Misha Rudominski, Himera’s co-founder and chief executive.

“We are starting by testing technologies in orbit, while our long-term goal is to develop capabilities that will strengthen the country’s strategic security and reduce dependence on external communications providers,” he said.
Himera, founded in 2022, develops secure tactical radio systems for military forces, including equipment designed to operate in environments affected by electronic warfare.
GomSpace, headquartered in Aalborg, Denmark, manufactures small satellites, communications payloads and spacecraft subsystems.

The companies said Obria Nano is operating in orbit and undergoing testing that will inform the design of a constellation. They did not disclose the satellite’s specifications, communications capacity, project financing or the number of satellites envisioned for the network.

Neither European initiative is expected to replace Starlink’s extensive global network. Smaller national constellations could provide dedicated communications for selected military operations while supplementing commercial services.

articles.title: Canelo returns to beat Mbilli and reclaim world title in Riyadh

paras.en: Canelo Alvarez returns to beat Christian Mbilli and reclaim WBC super-middleweight world championship in Riyadh

Canelo Alvarez outscores Christian Mbilli to win back WBC title in Riyadh; Jaime Munguia came close to disaster but retained the WBA super-middleweight title, beating Nikita Zon; Watch Chris Billam-Smith fight Cheavon Clarke on November 7 live on Sky Sports
Canelo Alvarez marshalled Christian Mbilli as he reclaimed the WBC super-middleweight world championship he used to hold.
The Mexican superstar won the title beating Mbilli by unanimous decision in Riyadh.
Canelo was returning to boxing a year after his stunning loss to Terence Crawford and went straight in with a strong, previously undefeated world champion.
Mbilli did press Alvarez in the first half of the fight. He threw in busy bursts and moved Canelo into the ropes.

Jaime Munguia had to weather an almighty scare to carve out a unanimous decision win over Nikita Zon and defend his WBA super-middleweight title.
Zon, genuinely an awkward southpaw, found a home for heavy backhand lefts in the opening rounds. He drove Munguia to the ropes and into corners.

He was on the verge of knocking out Munguia in the sixth round. He led with a long left uppercut, badly hurting the Mexican. Munguia retreated but Zon swarmed all over him. He hammered Munguia but the champion refused to fall.

articles.title: Hamilton: A 'dream' to emulate Schumacher with first Ferrari pole

paras.en: Lewis Hamilton says it's a 'dream' to emulate Michael Schumacher after claiming his first Ferrari pole at the Mexico City GP

Lewis Hamilton became F1's oldest pole-sitter in 44 years after claiming his first Ferrari pole at the Mexico City Grand Prix; the result secured a record-extending 105th career pole for the Brit; watch Sunday's race at 8pm (build-up from 6.30pm), live on Sky Sports F1
Lewis Hamilton said he had achieved his "dream" of emulating Michael Schumacher after claiming his first pole position for Ferrari at the Mexico City Grand Prix.
The 41-year-old unexpectedly snatched pole from Mercedes' George Russell in a thrilling end to qualifying to take his first pole in over three years and extend his record career pole tally to 105.

Hamilton and Schumacher share the sport's record for the most Drivers' Championships with seven each, but while the Brit won one title with McLaren and the other six with Mercedes, the bulk of Schumacher's success came at Ferrari as he won five in a row from 2000 to 2004.

Hamilton told Sky Sports F1: "To get the pole, finally get a pole for Ferrari, just takes me back to when I was a kid and sitting on the sofa and watching Michael get those poles, thinking 'how cool would it be to do that?'"
"It was a dream my family have shared with me and I know so many people in the world grew up watching Michael.
"To be at this point of my career and still have this special feeling - 105 [poles], the number doesn't mean much in a sense, it feels like the first.
"I spoke a couple years ago about getting to have a first. It feels like when you get to 40 they are all gone, but I'm having those firsts this year and I'm in a really good place."
2009 F1 world champion and Hamilton's former team-mate Jenson Button said he noticed how confident the Ferrari driver looked in Q3.
Hamilton had been four tenths off the pace of his team-mate Charles Leclerc after the first runs in Q3, but then produced his best lap of the weekend when it mattered most.
"Watching that lap back, he was so smooth," Button said.
"There was one moment were he got a bit of oversteer but apart from that he is driving within the limits. I think that's the big positive."

Hamilton, who is the oldest pole-sitter since Mario Andretti in 1982, starts on the front row alongside Russell - the only two drivers who can prevent Kimi Antonelli from becoming world champion on Sunday.
Antonelli only needs to finish in the top nine to become champion but, should he come 10th or fail to score any points, victory for Hamilton or Russell would delay the inevitable for another round.
The long run down to Turn 1 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez always creates jeopardy and the pole-sitter has the disadvantage of towing trailing cars down the long straight.

Hamilton, whose only Grand Prix win for Ferrari came in Barcelona earlier this year, says it will be a "big challenge" to keep Russell and Leclerc behind, but that he will make his car "as wide as possible".
"It's a long run down to Turn 1 - very tough," he said.
"It's not a bad place to be in first but people can tow you. Lando did a really good job last year so I have to try and do what he did.

"Getting away off the line, I'm going in a little bit blind because in FP2 the engine stopped, so I didn't get to do a long run. I really don't know what the balance is like when you put all that fuel in.

"I kind of have to engineer my way through it and somehow drive my way through it. If we can get to Turn 1 first, then it comes down to how you manage your tyres. Hopefully we can have one of those special days where you can maybe whisper them a long way."

Russell thinks Turn 1 will be "crucial" as overtaking is likely to be difficult due to the high altitude, with the tight margins between the top teams potentially too small for passes to be possible later in the race.
"I think the race pace, there's probably going to be a tenth between the top seven or eight drivers," Russell said.
"Overtaking is going to be tough, overheating, etc. It's always the case here in Mexico. But get a good night's sleep and see what the race brings."
Leclerc added: "I'll keep my head down as much as possible and see what's possible. But, yes, it's always an exciting Turn 1 there, and we'll see how it goes."

articles.title: Antonelli feeling 'tense' amid effort to seal F1 title

paras.en: Kimi Antonelli: Mercedes driver admits to feeling 'tense' amid effort to seal F1 title at Mexico City Grand Prix

Kimi Antonelli needs top-nine finish to become world champion at Mexico City Grand Prix; he only qualified fifth and was off the pace compared to Mercedes team-mate George Russell; watch Sunday's race at 8pm (build-up from 6.30pm), live on Sky Sports F1
Kimi Antonelli has admitted to feeling "more tense than usual" ahead of attempting to seal the Formula 1 world championship at Sunday's Mexico City Grand Prix.
The 20-year-old only needs to finish ninth in the race to become the sport's youngest world champion.
Antonelli qualified fifth on Saturday but will start from fourth on the grid due to a penalty for Max Verstappen.
Speaking after the session, the Italian revealed that he is not feeling his best as he continues to recover from an illness that caused him to miss his media duties on Thursday.
He told Sky Sports F1: "It has not been the easiest weekend to be fair.
"Definitely still not feeling 100 per cent. There is talk of what could happen [with the championship] and definitely I'm a bit more tense than usual.
"Definitely I don't feel as relaxed but I try to have a good sleep tonight and focus on tomorrow."
Despite his condition, Antonelli was still able to produce a decent final lap in qualifying as he finished within two tenths of pole-sitter Lewis Hamilton.
However, the fact that his team-mate George Russell was only marginally behind Hamilton in second perhaps reflected the Italian not being able to summon his best level.
Antonelli added: "I struggled to get a good feeling from the tyres in Q3. I just didn't have the most confidence. I was a bit tense, I am not going to lie.
"It was a poor lap, many mistakes here and there. Overall, still P4 and a lot to play for tomorrow."
'It's insane!' - Norris happy to pass No 1 onto Antonelli
Lando Norris says he is "more than happy" to pass the number one he has had on his McLaren this year to Antonelli when the Mercedes driver replaces him as world champion.
Antonelli has massively exceeded expectations during just his second season in F1 to comprehensively outperform Russell, who began the year as the clear title favourite.
"He's done an incredible job and done it in a pretty incredible way," Norris said ahead of the race weekend in Mexico.
"People are saying he hasn't had any tough competition this year. That proves the point that he's done such an incredible job.
"He's got a very, very talented team-mate that he's beaten through the whole season.
"I have nothing but respect for Kimi. He's a very nice guy. We get along very well and I'm more than happy to pass the No 1 over to him.
"He deserves it. He's done an incredible job, especially in his second year in Formula 1. Youngest world champion, it's pretty insane.
"I enjoy other people having that kind of success. It's nice to see."
