articles.title: U.S. approves $2.1 billion sale of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine
articles.author: Abigail Williams

paras.en: The Trump administration approved the sale of $2.1 billion in Patriot air defense systems to Ukraine on Friday, the State Department said in a statement.
The State Department said 500 Patriot missiles are being purchased for Ukraine with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through a U.S. program and that no American funds were involved.

“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe,” the department said in a news release.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said repeatedly in recent weeks that Patriot missile systems are essential for defending against Russian attacks.

“Our soldiers have been very strong this year. Then we really build, try to build air defense shield to defend our civilians, but always a big deficit with Patriot missiles and other kind of air defense,” Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” two weeks ago.
The Ukrainian leader had accused the Pentagon of delaying the delivery of the interceptor missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine.
The announcement of the sale comes as President Donald Trump has recently ramped up criticism of Zelenskyy and described him as an obstacle to efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Zelenskyy also recently noted that Ukraine was left further exposed because of restrictions on the Starlink satellite internet service.

Ukraine said Saturday that both Starlink, run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and its military variant, Starshield, were fully functional after a long outage, two days after Trump indicated Musk had been asked to “put it back.”

articles.title: Massive protests sweep Europe over cost of living and strained public services
articles.author: Freddie Clayton

paras.en: Massive protests were sweeping Europe on Saturday as part of demonstrations driven by the cost of living and deficient public services, with police bracing for potential violence after recent looting and riots.
Germany, France, Spain and Italy are among the nations where demonstrations were being held on Halloween following a recent wave of Gen Z-led marches across the continent.

French officials said they would deploy 70,000 police on Saturday following some of the worst rioting in decades, which erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education evolved into wider demonstrations about the cost of living and social security.
As the demonstrations began Saturday afternoon in Paris, protesters were pictured holding a banner that read: “We do not need tear gas for our future to be blurry.”
Videos vetted by NBC News show large crowds and fires burning in Marseille.

Some 320,000 people demonstrated across France on Saturday, including 70,000 in Paris, according to the French Interior Ministry. Authorities reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night.

While the protests have been largely peaceful, police arrested 1,300 people last week after an estimated 410,000 took to the streets in cities across the country. Stores, public buildings and businesses have also been damaged since the protests erupted last month.

“Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said at a news conference earlier this week as he set out security arrangements, adding there was “a very high risk” of unrest.
Measures introduced last week to protect shops would be reinforced, he said, and demonstrations would not be permitted “in city centers, where there is a risk of public disorder.”
The U.S. Embassy in France advised travelers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned.

The protests in France began after Prime Minister Emmanuel Macron launched budget talks for 2027. Students in the country, angry over a declining education system and the high cost of living, then took to the streets.
They were later joined by unions and the Yellow Vests, a grassroots movement that emerged in 2018 as a revolt against fuel taxes.
Those demonstrations appear to have inspired similar protests across the continent, with protests erupting in Belgium, Spain, Italy and elsewhere.
In Germany there were demonstrations organized by the campaign group Gen Z regelt (Gen Z takes charge) in more than 30 cities Saturday, including the capital Berlin and the financial hub Frankfurt.
The groups demand spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and are against plans to return to mandatory military service.

“We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, whose capital is Frankfurt.
Protesters gathered in front of Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate, as police said an additional 1,500 officers would be deployed throughout the city.
While most people rallied peacefully, some protests turned violent on Saturday night.

In downtown Frankfurt, some rioters smashed several storefronts and stole goods from inside. They also stole weapons from a gun store, which police were able to retrieve later. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.

Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.

In the United Kingdom, hundreds of demonstrators are expected to gather outside the U.S. Embassy in London on Saturday and risk arrest in support of Palestine Action, a protest group banned by the British government.
In Serbia, student-led activism also helped unseat the country’s long-time leader at the ballot box.

In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year after groups of masked protesters looted stores in the fashion capital and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police earlier this month.
Tens of thousands of people again took to the streets of Rome on Friday and other cities and towns across the country.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful, but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protesters and groups of police charging to disperse protesters.
Italian police were out in force with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the capital.

“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” said Luca, a 20-year-old medical student who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.

articles.title: Queensland's 28th governor sworn in at parliament house
articles.author: Stephen Clarke

paras.en: Justice Thomas Bradley has been sworn in as Queensland's 28th governor in a ceremony at the state's parliament.
Justice Bradley served on the Supreme Court from 2018 and moved to the Court of Appeal in 2025.
He replaces Dr Jeanette Young as Queensland's governor.
Justice Thomas Bradley has been sworn in as Queensland's 28th governor in the state's parliament.
In his first address as governor, Justice Bradley said he and his partner, Dr Matthew Yoong, looked forward to engaging with people across Queensland.
"We aim to spend as much time out of Brisbane as we spend in it," he said.
"To help harness the wisdom, the skill and the goodwill that is in every community as we all answer the call of the Olympic motto, which is to go faster, higher and stronger, together."
Premier David Crisafulli said the appointment marked a "significant moment" for Queensland.
Justice Bradley served on the Supreme Court from 2018 and moved to the Court of Appeal in 2025.
Mr Crisafulli said Justice Bradley's experience in the law had given him "strong preparation" for the office.
"You have encountered people at some of the most difficult moments of their lives. You have listened to them, weighed decision of profound consequence and helped bring resolution."

Outside of his career in the courts, Justice Bradley has carried out roles including as chair of the Brisbane Festival Giving Committee, ambassador for the Pinnacle Foundation, and on the Gallery of Modern Art Foundation Committee.
Opposition Leader Steven Miles said the state was stronger when people in public roles reflected the community.
"That is the Queensland we are all proud of and the Queensland His Excellency represents."
Outgoing governor Dr Jeanette Young said she departed the role with a "profound sense of gratitude and pride".
"Serving the people of Queensland as governor has been one of the greatest honours and privileges of my life," she said.
Prior to her role as governor, Dr Young served as Queensland's chief health officer during the COVID-19 pandemic.
During her time as governor, Dr Young said she had travelled to all 77 local government areas in Queensland and visited each of the state's public hospitals.
She granted royal assent to 168 pieces of legislation, attended 257 consecutive council meetings and welcomed more than 114 diplomatic representatives from overseas.
Dr Young said Queensland's government house had welcomed more than 100,000 visitors during her time in the role.
"As I leave here today I have every confidence that government house will continue to evolve, serve and reflect the very best of Queensland," Dr Young said.

articles.title: Suns miss top four by a whisker despite win over Giants

paras.en: Gold Coast won its final game of the home and away season, but left the field shattered after letting slip the double chance in the finals.
The Suns needed a solid win to boost their percentage sufficiently to replace Carlton in fourth spot after the Blues' win over Brisbane on Saturday.
But instead their 9.8 (62) to 7.11 (53) victory at Henson Park left them just 0.2 percentage points behind Carlton.
GWS could be proud of its efforts, having fought hard before a home crowd to send off the retiring Alicia Eva and Isabel Huntington at their final game.
Eva was an inaugural AFLW player 10 years ago with Collingwood and served as the Giants' captain for five years.
Huntington was a number one draft pick and All-Australian, though three separate ACL injuries plagued her six-year career.

It seemed it was going to be a walk in the park for the Suns, who dominated the first half around the stoppage and in midfield and led the clearances 16-10 thanks to Charlie Rowbottom and Lucy Single, who had five each.
But the Giants came out with a bang in the third quarter.
They led disposals 68–46 and converted from eight of their 10 entries inside-50, kept the Suns scoreless and took an 11-point lead before the final term.
Rowbottom did everything she could in the fourth quarter to claw back the lead and kicked a goal in the dying minutes to put the Suns back in front.
She ended with 33 disposals, two goals and 12 clearances, but didn't have much to celebrate after the Suns' ninth win of the season.
"Obviously we're happy to get away with the four points, but I wanted to finish fourth," Rowbottom said post-game.
Meanwhile, Essendon's 4.14 (38) to 4.7 (31) win over Collingwood handed outgoing Bombers coach Natalie Wood one last win and Pies boss Sam Wright one final loss.

articles.title: Epstein survivor thinks serial sex offender would be 'proud'
articles.author: David Marchese

paras.en: Epstein survivor Lisa Phillips says there’s "no way" the disgraced financier took his own life in prison, adding to doubts that have sparked conspiracy theories.
The podcast host says it's time the world focuses on how to stamp out widespread sexual abuse in society.
Lisa Phillips says she's trying to move on with her life after months of advocacy for Epstein survivors around the world.
Every time Lisa Phillips is on her phone, she knows she will see a picture of the man who abused her, Jeffrey Epstein.
"I'm on Instagram, TikTok, his face always pops up," she says.
"I do what I need to do but I don't want to look at his face."

More than a year after Ms Phillips joined dozens of other Epstein survivors on Capitol Hill, sharing their experiences publicly for the first time and demanding the release of the Epstein files, the podcast host is reflecting on the "interesting" turn her life has taken.
"I'm feeling a lot better now than I was about a year ago," she tells triple j hack.
"I have a lot of answered questions, things that I was really curious about since my early 20s.
"I don't regret it because it's actually where I found myself again and got my power back."
Lisa Phillips is one of hundreds of Epstein survivors.
She first met the disgraced businessman on his private island in 2000, when she was working as a model.
Like many others, she describes a cycle of grooming and abuse that continued for years, until she was finally able to get away from the sex offender in 2004.
Now, seven years after Epstein's death, and months after millions of documents, images and videos related to the financier were made public, she's relieved.
"Everything that I had known was in those files, so it validated it all for me," she says.
"But many of my survivor sisters' names weren't redacted — their addresses, their emails, pictures.
"It was pretty dirty what they did to them."
While the US Department of Justice maintains it has published all significant records under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, there is ongoing debate about what has not been released.
"There's a lot that people don't know," Ms Phillips tells hack.
"I think the Department of Justice just doesn't know what to do because there's so much to go through.
"But there's a lot more to look into, that's for sure."
Conspiracy theories around the death of Jeffrey Epstein in his New York jail cell in August 2019 continue to captivate the world.
Whether or not his death was self-inflicted, as determined by the New York City medical examiner and federal investigations, sparks furious discussions online.
Many, including Epstein's brother and lawyer, have publicly stated they do not believe the sex offender took his own life.
"Absolutely not. No way," she tells hack.
"I don't believe he killed himself because I just felt like he always knew that he would get away with it.
"I think he had too many people behind him to help him get away.
"So no, I don't believe that for a second."
When asked what she believes Jeffrey Epstein would say if he was alive today, Ms Phillips pauses, knowing that her answer will not only surprise but confuse a lot of people.
"When I was with my survivor sisters last … we thought of that … if Jeffrey was alive and he walked in the room right now, what would he say?
"We thought that he would be proud of us."
Ms Phillips says that reaction is indicative of the power of grooming.
"He groomed us to think of him … as a mentor type," she says.
"It's almost like we think he would say, 'Wow, you didn't just stay silent, you're standing up for yourselves.'
"I know it's kind of ironic, but I think that's actually what he would say.
"I do think people, men, weren't expecting that … because they like you to live in your shame and live in your silence."
After a break from advocacy to protect her mental health, Lisa Phillips is throwing herself into her podcast, From Now On, where she speaks with other survivors, experts and changemakers.
"We have a big problem all around the world, in Australia too … with sexual abuse in our society," she says.
Ms Phillips says she has been overwhelmed with the response from other survivors flooding her inbox with their own experiences.
Many of them are men, speaking about abuse that happened to them as children.
She says it's a good reminder for young people to "use their voice" to protect themselves.
"If something happens to you … immediately go tell somebody. I just stayed silent and kept that shame and didn't want to say anything."
"But your mental health, it will destroy you if you keep things inside."
After a year of public campaigning, travel and advocacy, Lisa Phillips says she is looking forward to getting on with the rest of her life.
"It's kind of hard because now I wear a hat … I'm just like, 'Oh great, I am the Epstein survivor.'
"That's not really what I wanted to be in life."
But she admits speaking out has given her a self-belief she never knew existed.
"When people say, 'I am proud of you' or, 'You're so brave because you spoke up,' that's really nice."
Ms Phillips says she's now in a "good place" and is looking forward to finding purpose by supporting other survivors.
"It makes me feel really good changing lives, seeing them getting into a healthy relationship and having a beautiful life," she says.

articles.title: Judge throws out Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter

paras.en: Judge throws out Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
Ruling says U.S. president was 'grasping at straws,' dismisses lawsuit with prejudice

Saying the president was "grasping at straws," a U.S. federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump's $10-billion lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to wealthy financier Jeffrey Epstein.
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law.
The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the Journal's investigative reporting.
When a case is thrown out "with prejudice," it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.
The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term.
- Trump sues Wall Street Journal reporters, owners after Epstein story, court records show
- Wall Street Journal asks judge to toss Trump lawsuit over Epstein story

In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.
Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them "fake news" and insults their journalists.

The lawsuit was over a story the Journal published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter that the paper said bore Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday.

The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump.

The letter bearing Trump's name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, "Happy Birthday - and may every day be another wonderful secret," according to the newspaper.
Trump denied writing it and called the story "false, malicious, and defamatory."

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having "knowingly and recklessly" published "numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements," which, it alleged, caused "overwhelming financial and reputational harm" to the president.

Gayles previously dismissed the suit in April, saying Trump had failed to make the argument that the article was published with the intent to be malicious. But he gave the president a chance to file an amended complaint, which he did in May.

In Saturday's ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court's landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth.
"The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice," Gayles wrote.

"Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false."
The judge also noted that the Journal's story did not ignore or minimize Trump's denial, "Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it."
Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit.

articles.title: NASA telescope predicted to plunge back to Earth after failed rescue mission

paras.en: NASA telescope predicted to plunge back to Earth after failed rescue mission
Years of intense solar activity dragged Swift down faster than usual
An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower.
The U.S. Space Force predicts the Swift Observatory will come crashing down on or around Friday.

Most of the 1.5-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive re-entry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission's chief scientist.

Any surviving wreckage will most likely plunge into the ocean. But swaths of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the re-entry zone. The Space Force is tracking the telescope's dwindling path.

Its cosmic cremation has the Swift team mourning yet full of gratitude for the observations the telescope made during its 22 years in orbit. Swift blasted off on Nov. 20, 2004, to search for some of the biggest explosions in the universe: gamma ray bursts and supernovas.
Workers look at the final pieces of protective cover on the Swift spacecraft that must be removed at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in September 2002. (NASA/The Associated Press)

"We've known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic," said Pennsylvania State University's John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team.

Intense solar activity over the past few years dragged Swift down faster than usual. NASA hired Katalyst Space a year ago to mount a rush rescue. But the company's three-armed robot named Link ran into trouble after launching in July and got no closer than 12 to 15 kilometres to the telescope. Link plunged back to Earth in September.

Swift resumed observations once the rescue attempt was called off, discovering even more gamma ray bursts and other ultra high-energy events. But by late October, the telescope was too low to remain steady for observations, and its systems were shut down.

Its final tally: more than 2,000 gamma ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, not to mention a slew of comets, asteroids and star-shredding black holes. The telescope's superpower was its ability to swivel swiftly — thus its name — toward erupting celestial events.

NASA considered Swift a first responder for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes and others that would follow its alerts and provide deeper investigations. Scientists are still figuring out how to fill the gap.
"Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe," Nousek said in an email.

articles.title: Binance says billions replaced from hack that FBI blames on North Korea

paras.en: Binance says billions replaced from hack that FBI blames on North Korea
'We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets,' says cryptocurrency exchange
Crypto exchange Binance said on Saturday it has been able to replace 90 per cent of the amount stolen after a record $6.3-billion US hack of its platform by using company money to buy new tokens.
The remaining 10 per cent consists of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X.

"We've now replenished 90 per cent of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10 per cent. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X on Saturday.

Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance — the world's biggest crypto exchange — sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe after losing more than $6 billion worth of crypto in a hack that analysts and the FBI blamed on North Korea.

The FBI on Saturday said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Members of the unit were observed by law enforcement converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ethereum, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expects "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology.

Teng said on Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.
After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds, but it said on Saturday it was still on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday.
- Binance says $6.3B US hacked in what could be largest cryptocurrency theft ever
- Trump pardons Canadian Binance CEO who failed to stop illegal activity on crypto platform
Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses.

The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X.
Binance also said it had taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 00:00 GMT on Oct. 31, as part of its proof-of-reserves process.

Users holding the 10 listed tokens — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC — would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum ratio of 1:1 once the full proof was available, it said.

articles.title: Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience

paras.en: Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.

Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practising "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."
Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.

On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.
Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."

The List, which emerged from the student revolt, is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote, leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.

Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.

The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime.

The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died. The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.
Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.

"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."

Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition, and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.
How much damage can the old government do to the new one?

It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia, an organization that monitors the work of governments.

The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.

However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."

In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.

The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focussed on making changes in domestic politics, and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.

Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.

"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.

Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.

The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: FBI says North Korea behind $6 billion Binance crypto theft

paras.en: The FBI said Saturday that North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6 billion (€5.36 billion) in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

"The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the US law enforcement agency said in a statement.
The theft, which happened within a matter of minutes, is believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency heist in history.
The stolen assets included bitcoin, ethereum and stablecoins such as tether and USD Coin, whose values are pegged to traditional currencies.
News of the cyberattack caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to slump on Friday.
The FBI said the theft was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.
The agency said it had "observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets" primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum.

"It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi [decentralized finance] and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages," it added.
The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to ensure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.
The exchange said on Saturday it was using company funds worth over $6.34 billion to buy tokens to replenish about 90% of the assets stolen in the attack.
The remaining 10% consisted of tokens that were less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy back, the company said.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.
The heist came amid growing worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

articles.title: Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino weather pattern

paras.en: Bolivia has declared a nationwide state of emergency to free up resources to deal with the effects of the El Nino weather phenomenon.
Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz signed the decree on Saturday, which also called for further deployments of rescue teams in areas of the country hard hit by flooding and drought.
El Nino will have “very severe impacts in terms of drought and floods”, Paz said, adding that Bolivia needs “the cooperation of all institutions”.
Drought is now affecting 78,000 families in six of Bolivia’s nine departments and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle, according to a government report this week.
Bolivia is also prone to flooding. In December 2025, floods in the Santa Cruz region killed dozens of people.
Neighbouring Chile’s capital, Santiago, recorded the rainiest October ever, while wildfires in Peru killed at least 12 people last month.
El Nino, a global climate phenomenon that occurs roughly every two to seven years, is part of the planet’s natural weather cycle.
During this climate event, warming in the Pacific Ocean brings worldwide changes in winds, pressure, and rainfall patterns, often causing extreme weather.

El Nino’s intensity varies, and its impact changes based on geographic location, but this cycle could be the strongest in recorded history. It is due to peak at the end of 2026, but its impacts could continue well into 2027.
Scientists predict El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths globally, with the poorest countries worst impacted.
In early September, the World Meteorological Organization reported a nearly 100 percent likelihood that El Nino will continue through February 2027.

articles.title: UN demands investigation after staffer’s death in Houthi custody in Yemen

paras.en: The United Nations has demanded an investigation into the death of an employee in Houthi detention in Yemen.

Mohammad el-Shami, a staff member of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) in Yemen, died more than a month ago, but his family was only recently informed, the UN said in a statement on Saturday.
The Houthis did not say how he died, but his family “deserve to know the truth”, said UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk.
The human rights chief also demanded “full transparency” from the Houthi authorities and an “urgent, independent and thorough investigation” into el-Shami’s death.

El-Shami had been arbitrarily held in Houthi custody since June 2024, when he and more than 60 people working with the UN and other NGOs were detained and accused of being part of an “American-Israeli spy network”.

“I am also gravely concerned” for the seven other OHCHR personnel who were detained alongside el-Shami and are still being held, Turk said. “I appeal again for their immediate and unconditional release.”
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a separate statement on Saturday that he was “appalled” by el-Shami’s death and echoed Turk’s calls for an investigation.
The UN is “urgently seeking answers” from the group about the circumstances of his death, Guterres added.
El-Shami is the second UN staff member to die in Houthi detention, following the death of a World Food Programme staffer in February 2025.
A total of 72 UN staffers and NGO workers, including el-Shami, have been detained by the Houthis.
The UN paused operations in parts of Houthi-held Yemen in February 2025 over concerns for the safety of its employees.
The rebel group has previously paraded some detainees on television channels, presenting them as collaborators with Western intelligence agencies and Israel.
On October 6, the UN announced that a World Food Programme employee had been released after being “arbitrarily detained” by the Iran-backed group.

articles.title: ‘Like Kashmir’: How a toxic marble dump yard became a tourist spot in India

paras.en: Kishangarh, India – As Bagharam Gurjar kneels to pull weeds from his maize field in western India’s Rajasthan state, the sound of his wife coughing nearby makes him restless.
“Everything gets ruined when dust settles on the soil,” says Gurjar, 53, barely looking up.
“May God make everything right,” replies his wife between bouts of chronic cough. “Otherwise, it becomes difficult to grow crops.”
The Gurjars are among nearly 5,000 people living in the vicinity of what has turned out to be one of the most unusual tourist destinations in India.

Their village, Bhogiyawas, is just 6km (4 miles) from Kishangarh, where a 300-acre (121-hectare) marble slurry dumping yard resembles a snow-clad landscape, attracting hundreds of tourists every day in an otherwise arid state.

Locally known as a “Snow Yard”, the landfill in Rajasthan’s Ajmer district is the largest of its kind in Asia. Its pristine white hills and slopes with water-filled pits provide a surreal backdrop for visitors, who get free entry to the site.

Newlyweds pose against the snowy backdrop or the blue artificial lake, while couples soon to get married organise pre-wedding photoshoots. Social media influencers throng the landfill to make reels. Music videos and movies are also frequently shot here.

“Everyone, right from my five-year-old niece to my mother, loves it very much. Their first impression was that this looks like Kashmir,” Salim Shahzada, a businessman from Uttar Pradesh state, told Al Jazeera, referring to Indian-administered Kashmir.
Shahzada said he had visited the place a couple of times and decided to bring his family along this time. But he had no idea about the health and environmental problems linked to the dumping yard.
“I do not have much knowledge about this place or its ill effects. I only know that this is where marble cutting waste is dumped and that the hill itself is made of this waste,” he said.

Kishangarh, a marble and granite hub, is home to nearly 1,200 processing units, with the total daily business estimated at more than 160 million rupees ($1.7m), providing jobs to about 25,000 people, according to the Federation of Indian Granite and Stone Industry.

Every day, nearly 1,000 tankers carry slurry from those units and empty roughly 5,500 tonnes of waste on the government-allotted dump site, which, for the people living nearby, has turned into a health hazard.
Gurjar said the yard has affected residents in at least six villages. “How many problems can I even tell you about? If there were just one or two, we could deal with them,” he said.

“But here, almost everything is going wrong because of the dumping yard. People like me are suffering from chest infections, dental problems and skin allergies. It does not matter whether they are children or elderly people; everyone is suffering.”
Gurjar said he and his wife are forced to take regular medicines for chest infections or skin problems.

Aditi Goyal, a general physician at Ajmer’s Ganga Narayan Hospital, said the residents of Kishangarh face several health risks, mainly respiratory and skin problems. She said the workers in the marble processing units are more vulnerable to chronic illnesses because of prolonged exposure to toxic dust.
“Over the last couple of years, cases of respiratory problems have increased significantly in this area because people are exposed to dust from the dumping yard,” Goyal told Al Jazeera.

“However, dust from industrial waste is not the only issue. People in Kishangarh, who are mostly farmers, also suffer from infections caused by dust coming from the soil,” she said, advising people to wear masks to protect themselves from dust.
The same dust settles on the fields, hardening the soil and making it difficult to grow crops.

A study led by Laxmi Kant Sharma, professor in the department of environmental science at the Central University of Rajasthan, found that the concentration of lead silicate in Kishangarh’s soil was several times higher than normal, indicating extreme contamination.
“Since the waste particles are smaller than 75 micrometres, they can spread far and wide, making the soil infertile,” the study said.

The study also found that the concentration of PM2.5 exceeds the limit of ambient air quality standards. “Several people may be suffering from silicosis. The government needs to take immediate action to prevent the situation from getting out of hand,” it said.

Ugam Singh, another resident of Bhogiyawas, remembers when things were different. The continuous dumping of slurry slowly changed the landscape and the lives of people in Kishangarh, says the 65-year-old.
“Nowadays, the situation has worsened to such an extent that even the groundwater is no longer fit for consumption,” Singh said.

“The fluoride levels in the water are so high that it tastes salty. My teeth have started decaying and my bones have become weak,” he added, pointing to his teeth, which appeared pale, pitted and worn.

Singh said the residents of villages surrounding the dump yard have complained to the authorities, including officials of the Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board (RSPCB). But their requests fell on deaf ears.

“What I have come to understand is that it does not matter which government is in power. No one listens to the poor. To make the rich richer, the government sacrifices the interests of people like us. It feels as though our lives have no value,” Singh said.
“Even today all we want is for this marble slurry dumping to stop so that we can breathe freely again and our fields can become green and productive once again.”
Singh also claims that if residents of all the villages around the dumping yard were properly examined, almost every household would have someone suffering from respiratory problems such as asthma.

Last year, local environmentalist Drupad Malik filed a case before the National Green Tribunal over the harmful health and environmental effects of the Kishangarh dumping yard. The tribunal observed that unregulated dumping of marble slurry was contaminating groundwater and air. It directed the RSPCB to enforce monitoring, conduct sample inspections and penalise the marble processing units violating environmental norms.
Al Jazeera reached out to a senior official at the RSPCB’s regional office in Kishangarh, but she refused to speak on the matter.

Central University’s Sharma said the areas surrounding the Kishangarh dumping yard are unfit for human settlement. He said his research was shared with state authorities, but nothing was done to improve the environmental conditions in the area.

“There is a dire need to shift the dumping yard to another place where there is no human contact. This area has become extremely toxic and vulnerable to severe diseases. I am surprised that people are allowed to visit the site without masks and even have food there,” Sharma told Al Jazeera.
“I have forwarded several suggestions, including installing tile units, as [marble] slurry is used in tile manufacturing. This could, to some extent, help reduce pollution in Kishangarh,” he added.
Meanwhile, Ram Lal, a resident of Tokra village, about a 15-minute drive from Bhogiyawas, appealed to the government to find an alternative site for dumping the marble slurry.
“Kishangarh is full of slurry, and it is time to shift the dumping yard out of here to some other place where no one will suffer for at least two to three decades,” Lal told Al Jazeera.
“We also demand that free medical camps be set up to assess people whose health has declined because of the fine dust particles that have been flying in the air and settling here for years,” he said.
“No one from our village can afford it if someone develops a disease that costs thousands of rupees to treat.”

articles.title: France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
articles.author: The Associated Press

paras.en: France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
PARIS — Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.

France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.
Authorities in France reported about 300 arrests nationwide so far — down from 800 at the same point in last week's protests.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.

At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.

The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.
Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.

Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."

The crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, the ring of avenues that skirts the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, a painter at work along the route drew cheers from the crowd, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city.

Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell.
Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris.

The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.

While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.

Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.

Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
Protests took place in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands

In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
In Berlin, young protesters also gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

Later on Saturday, police ended a protest march early in the western city of Cologne after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police also used water cannons to disperse demonstrators. In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds in Hamburg. In Frankfurt, protesters pummeled police with stones, injuring several officers, one of them severely, police said.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.

Thousands of protesters, including families with small children, converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal's housing crisis, holding up placards reading "Houses or Fire" and "We are not Afraid." Others in the crowd held aloft small cardboard houses while a few dressed up for Halloween.

In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting. However, there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances by midafternoon. Police frisked some groups of black-clad youngsters and checked their identities, local media reported. Many stores in the city were boarded up as a precaution.

articles.title: A new political era in the Southern Philippines
articles.author: Jan Camenzind Broomby

paras.en: A new political era in the Southern Philippines
A new local government has taken its seat in the southern Philippines, in a step that marks a milestone in the peace process for a conflict that has lasted some 80 years.

A new political era began on Friday in the Southern Philippines. Lawmakers took their seats in a newly elected local parliament, marking a major milestone in ending one of the country's last separatist insurgencies. It lasted eight decades and claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. Last month, reporter Jan Camenzind Broomby was at the polling stations as former fighters traded weapons for ballots. And a warning, this story has sounds of gunfire.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: (Non-English language spoken).
UNIDENTIFIED CROWD #1: (Non-English language spoken).

JAN CAMENZIND BROOMBY, BYLINE: In the Southern Philippines, a university gymnasium in Cotabato City has been transformed. Instead of sports fans, the stands teem with attendees of a grand political rally. Hundreds of supporters for the political wing of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, or MILF, a local Islamist militant group.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: (Non-English language spoken).
CAMENZIND BROOMBY: Mingling in the crowd, dozens of men who call themselves mujahideen fighters.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Yeah. All of us. We are all combatant.
CAMENZIND BROOMBY: Among them, Bhong Dalama.
BHONG DALAMA: We fight them in the battlefield.
CAMENZIND BROOMBY: He's a deputy base commander for the MILF who once fought a guerrilla war against the Philippine government.

CAMENZIND BROOMBY: Manila may have viewed it as a secessionist conflict, but to him, it was a form of jihad, a term whose meaning is contested globally, but many here interpret as a religious struggle to defend one's own beliefs. Now, after years of armed insurgency for the sake of the next generation, he hopes for peace.
DALAMA: We are more than willing to accept, based on the peaceful means.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #3: (Singing in non-English language).
CAMENZIND BROOMBY: The Philippines might be almost 79% Roman Catholic, but here in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, also known as the BARMM, Muslims are in the majority.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #3: (Singing in non-English language).

CAMENZIND BROOMBY: Locals have fought for autonomy for hundreds of years, including against the United States, which colonized the region in 1898, and then against the Philippines government after independence in 1946, which many people here viewed as a continuation of outside rule.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #4: (Non-English language spoken).
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #5: (Non-English language spoken).
CAMENZIND BROOMBY: A key figure in the struggle, Murad Ebrahim, chairperson of the MILF. In one of the Rebel group's strongholds, he tells us the time for violence is now over.
MURAD EBRAHIM: The real meaning of Jihad is struggle. We have struggled so much. We even wage war.

CAMENZIND BROOMBY: Under a peace deal signed in 2014, the MILF and Manila have agreed that BARMM will stay Filipino, but will have its own local government. Ebrahim says jihadi struggle, once expressed through violence, will now be expressed via democracy.
EBRAHIM: So now we have our own government, and we have to protect it. And this can only be protected by the balance.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #6: (Singing in non-English language).
CAMENZIND BROOMBY: As the morning prayers ring out on election day, we head to a polling station.
There's a queue that stretches all the way around the corner, with probably hundreds of people lining up.
Inside, we find Mohammed Bedtikan, a Cotabato local.
MOHAMMED BEDTIKAN: I feel great because this the first parliamentary election here in BARMM. We're hoping that this election will be safe.

CAMENZIND BROOMBY: And the fears, they're valid because in the last few hours, there have been two explosions in this city alone and numerous people shot dead in what is thought to be election-related violence.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #7: A ba da ba da ba.
CAMENZIND BROOMBY: A reminder that even though lawmakers are now taking their seats, peace is fragile.
GEORGI ENGELBRECHT: The interim government has failed to curb violence.

CAMENZIND BROOMBY: This is Georgi Engelbrecht, from the Belgium-based think tank International Crisis Group. He says combatants must now build political coalitions that deliver for locals, because after the votes are counted, no party has won a clear majority.
ENGELBRECHT: If malgovernance will persist, it might be just a matter of time until a new group will emerge and fight for the rights of the people.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #8: (Non-English language spoken).
CAMENZIND BROOMBY: And another challenge. While some 26,000 of the MILF's combatants have been decommissioned, 14,000 remain active, guarding militia camps.
EBRAHIM: What we are asking now is that they will deliver...
CAMENZIND BROOMBY: Chairperson Ebrahim says decommissioning will continue once Manila provides mujahideen fighters with the support needed to reintegrate into society...
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #9: (Non-English language spoken).
UNIDENTIFIED CROWD #2: (Non-English language spoken).
CAMENZIND BROOMBY: ...With the hope that the fate of their homeland can now be decided not on the battlefield, but at the ballot box instead.
For NPR News, I'm Jan Camenzind Broomby in Cotabato City, the Philippines.
(SOUNDBITE OF 99GINGER AND C-AFROBRASIL'S "NOTURNO")

articles.title: Secretary Rubio has a tough time getting officials at G20 on the same page
articles.author: Michele Kelemen

paras.en: Secretary Rubio has a tough time getting officials at G20 on the same page
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, with a focus on economic and security challenges.
Tensions flared this weekend at a meeting chaired by Secretary of State Marco Rubio of the Group of 20 leading economies. NPR's Michele Kelemen reports from Atlanta.

MICHELE KELEMEN, BYLINE: There was no joint communiqué or even a family photo. Several foreign ministers did not want to be in a picture with Russia's Sergey Lavrov. So Rubio canceled plans for that, but he says countries did come together around some big themes, including freedom of navigation.

MARCO RUBIO: Safe passage of vessels in international waters is vital to the livelihood of the world. And we now live in a world where the Iranian regime actively and openly targets commercial vessels.
KELEMEN: He says the U.S. is open to diplomacy with Iran, but he wouldn't rule out a new round of attacks, even as the U.S. military tries to keep the Strait of Hormuz open.

RUBIO: Central Command in the United States has done a phenomenal job of protecting this shipping. And today, the amount of fuel getting through there is comparable with what was coming out before the conflict. But nonetheless, we've had to defend these ships from drones and missiles almost every single night.

KELEMEN: Other G20 countries are worried about the potential for a new escalation in the Middle East. Europeans are also nervous about U.S. sanctions relief to Russia. Germany's foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, is trying to highlight the positive, saying, while they may not agree on tactics, everyone shares the goal of getting Russia to the negotiating table to end the war in Ukraine.
JOHANN WADEPHUL: In the substance, we have the same position, not only in Europe, but together also with the United States of America. And for us, Marco Rubio was always a reliable partner.

KELEMEN: Rubio did meet briefly with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who's been making light over the dispute over the family photo and defending Russia's war in Ukraine. Russia has long blamed the West for provoking Moscow. Poland's foreign minister, Radek Sikorski, has heard it all before.
RADEK SIKORSKI: Sergey Lavrov's repeated diatribes against Europe suggests to me that they've realized that Europe has cards.

KELEMEN: Europe, he says, has Russia's frozen assets, and it's buying weapons from the U.S. for Ukraine. Poland is lobbying to become a member of the G20 over Russia's objections. Sikorski says he used his time here to push for a ceasefire in the Black Sea.
SIKORSKI: So that both Ukrainian and Russian grain could make it through the Bosphorus to the people who need it in Egypt and elsewhere.

KELEMEN: Secretary Rubio says he wouldn't place bets on whether such a ceasefire is possible, but he says there was a lot of interest around the table to do that. He also defended the decision to host Lavrov in Atlanta and to invite Russian president Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Florida, though it's not clear Putin will come.

RUBIO: We have to be able to talk to the Russian side, and one of the ways to do that is to invite him to forums like this, where they're not just hearing from us, but potentially hearing from other countries that are there as well.

KELEMEN: Secretary Rubio also met briefly with his counterpart from Brazil, breaking the ice after right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro lost the elections and fled to the U.S. Rubio says President Trump made the decision to allow Bolsonaro into the country, but the U.S. government did not facilitate the travel.
